title: Algebra 2
description: High school Algebra 2: function transformations, composition and inverses, complex numbers, nonlinear systems, systems in three variables and matrices, polynomial functions, radicals and rational exponents, rational expressions and functions, polynomial and rational inequalities, exponentials and logarithms, sequences and series, counting and the binomial theorem, probability and the normal distribution, and an introduction to the unit circle and trig graphs. Every lesson teaches with worked examples and graphs, and every skill has generated practice problems.
author: Erudior
changelog: Checked against university and open-textbook sources; corrected missing conditions in rules and definitions, and added a few short sections; new lessons on nonlinear systems, matrices, polynomial and rational inequalities, and the binomial theorem.

lessons.title: Transformations of parent functions
lessons.body:
Algebra 2 meets a lot of functions: quadratics, square roots, cubics, absolute values, reciprocals, exponentials and logarithms. You don't have to learn each graph from scratch. Most of them are a handful of basic shapes that have been slid, flipped or stretched, and each of those moves shows up in the formula in a predictable place. In Algebra 1 you saw one case of this: the vertex form $y = a(x - h)^2 + k$ puts the vertex of a parabola at $(h, k)$. This lesson makes that idea work for every function.

## Parent functions

A **[[parent function]]** is the simplest function in a family; every other member is built from it by changes to the formula. Here are the ones you'll use most. It's worth knowing each one's shape and a few exact points on it.

| Parent function | Formula | Key points | Domain | Range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Linear | $y = x$ | $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$ | all reals | all reals |
| Quadratic | $y = x^2$ | $(0, 0)$, $(\pm1, 1)$, $(\pm2, 4)$ | all reals | $y \ge 0$ |
| Cubic | $y = x^3$ | $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$, $(-1, -1)$ | all reals | all reals |
| Absolute value | $y = \lvert x \rvert$ | $(0, 0)$, $(\pm1, 1)$ | all reals | $y \ge 0$ |
| Square root | $y = \sqrt{x}$ | $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$, $(4, 2)$ | $x \ge 0$ | $y \ge 0$ |
| Cube root | $y = \sqrt[3]{x}$ | $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$, $(-8, -2)$ | all reals | all reals |
| Reciprocal | $y = \dfrac{1}{x}$ | $(1, 1)$, $(-1, -1)$ | $x \ne 0$ | $y \ne 0$ |
| Exponential | $y = 2^x$ | $(0, 1)$, $(1, 2)$ | all reals | $y > 0$ |

```plot
{"x": [-4, 4], "y": [-3, 5], "equal": true, "functions": [{"f": "x^2", "label": "y = x²"}, {"f": "abs(x)", "label": "y = |x|", "dashed": true}, {"f": "sqrt(x)", "from": 0, "to": 4, "label": "y = √x"}, {"f": "x^3", "label": "y = x³", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Four parent functions: the parabola, the V of |x|, the half-parabola √x, and the S-shaped cubic"}
```

A **[[transformation]]** changes a graph's position, orientation or size. There are three kinds: translations (slides), reflections (flips) and stretches or compressions. Throughout, $f$ is any function and $y = f(x)$ its graph.

## Translations

A **[[translation]]** slides the whole graph without turning or resizing it.

**[[Vertical shifts]]**. The graph of $y = f(x) + k$ is the graph of $f$ moved up $k$ units (down if $k < 0$). This one is easy to believe: every output gets $k$ added to it, so every point $(x, y)$ moves to $(x, y + k)$.

**[[Horizontal shifts]]**. The graph of $y = f(x - h)$ is the graph of $f$ moved right $h$ units (left if $h < 0$). The direction surprises people, so here's why. The new function at $x = h + 3$ gives $f(h + 3 - h) = f(3)$: it reaches the output that $f$ had at 3, but $h$ units later. Every point $(x, y)$ moves to $(x + h, y)$. So $y = \lvert x - 3 \rvert$ has its corner at $x = 3$ (the input that makes the inside zero), and $y = \lvert x + 3 \rvert = \lvert x - (-3) \rvert$ has its corner at $x = -3$.

A good rule of thumb: changes *outside* the function act on $y$ the way they look; changes *inside* act on $x$ the opposite way.

```plot
{"x": [-6, 6], "y": [-2, 6], "functions": [{"f": "abs(x)", "label": "y = |x|"}, {"f": "abs(x - 3)", "dashed": true, "label": "y = |x − 3|"}, {"f": "abs(x) + 2", "dashed": true, "label": "y = |x| + 2"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 0]}, {"at": [3, 0], "label": "(3, 0)"}, {"at": [0, 2], "label": "(0, 2)"}], "caption": "Subtracting 3 inside moves the graph right 3; adding 2 outside moves it up 2"}
```

## Reflections

A **[[reflection]]** flips the graph across a line, like a mirror image.

- $y = -f(x)$ reflects the graph across the $x$-axis: every output changes sign, so $(x, y) \to (x, -y)$.
- $y = f(-x)$ reflects the graph across the $y$-axis: the output that $f$ had at $x$ now appears at $-x$, so $(x, y) \to (-x, y)$.

For example, $y = -\sqrt{x}$ is the square root graph turned upside down (it heads down and to the right), while $y = \sqrt{-x}$ heads up and to the left, with domain $x \le 0$.

## Stretches and compressions

Multiplying the output by a positive number $a$ changes the graph's height. The graph of $y = a f(x)$ is a **[[vertical stretch]]** of the graph of $f$ by a factor of $a$ when $a > 1$ (every point moves away from the $x$-axis), and a **[[vertical compression]]** when $0 < a < 1$ (every point moves toward it). Points go $(x, y) \to (x, ay)$. A negative $a$ also reflects across the $x$-axis: $y = -3x^2$ is $y = x^2$ stretched by 3 and flipped.

Multiplying the *input* works the opposite way, as you'd expect from an inside change. The graph of $y = f(bx)$ with $b > 1$ is a **[[horizontal compression]]** by a factor of $\tfrac1b$: the function reaches each output $b$ times sooner, so $(x, y) \to \left(\tfrac{x}{b}, y\right)$. With $0 < b < 1$ it's a **[[horizontal stretch]]**. For example, $y = \sqrt{4x}$ reaches height 2 at $x = 1$ instead of $x = 4$.

For some parent functions a horizontal compression looks exactly like a vertical stretch: $(2x)^2 = 4x^2$ and $\sqrt{4x} = 2\sqrt{x}$. That's why most problems in this course use the vertical form $a f(x)$.

## Putting transformations together

The general form you'll see most is

$$y = a\,f(x - h) + k.$$

Read it as: stretch by $|a|$ (and reflect across the $x$-axis if $a < 0$), then shift right $h$ and up $k$. Each point of the parent graph moves by

$$(x, y) \to (x + h,\; ay + k).$$

The order matters for the $y$-coordinate: multiply by $a$ first, then add $k$. The point that sat at the parent's "anchor" (the vertex of $x^2$ or $\lvert x \rvert$, the endpoint of $\sqrt x$, the center of $x^3$) lands at $(h, k)$.

### Example 1

Graph $g(x) = -2\lvert x + 3 \rvert + 1$ and give its range.

1. Parent: $y = \lvert x \rvert$, a V with its corner at the origin.
2. Match the form $a f(x - h) + k$: $x + 3 = x - (-3)$, so $h = -3$; $a = -2$; $k = 1$.
3. Describe: stretch vertically by 2, reflect across the $x$-axis, shift left 3 and up 1.
4. Move three key points with $(x, y) \to (x - 3, -2y + 1)$:
   - $(0, 0) \to (-3, 1)$, the new corner;
   - $(1, 1) \to (-2, -1)$;
   - $(-1, 1) \to (-4, -1)$.
5. The V opens downward from $(-3, 1)$ with slopes $\pm 2$, so the highest output is 1: the range is $y \le 1$.

```plot
{"x": [-8, 2], "y": [-5, 3], "functions": [{"f": "abs(x)", "dashed": true, "label": "y = |x|"}, {"f": "-2*abs(x + 3) + 1", "label": "g(x) = −2|x + 3| + 1"}], "points": [{"at": [-3, 1], "label": "(−3, 1)"}, {"at": [-2, -1], "label": "(−2, −1)"}, {"at": [-4, -1], "label": "(−4, −1)"}], "caption": "The parent V is stretched, flipped, and moved so its corner lands at (−3, 1)"}
```

### Example 2

Write an equation for the square root graph that has been reflected across the $x$-axis, shifted left 4 and shifted up 3. State its domain and range.

1. Reflect: $y = -\sqrt{x}$.
2. Left 4 is an inside change of $+4$: $y = -\sqrt{x + 4}$.
3. Up 3 is an outside change: $g(x) = -\sqrt{x + 4} + 3$.
4. The endpoint $(0, 0)$ moves to $(-4, 3)$. The radicand must be nonnegative, so the domain is $x \ge -4$. The graph starts at height 3 and goes down, so the range is $y \le 3$.
5. Check another point: $(4, 2)$ on $y = \sqrt x$ moves to $(4 - 4, -2 + 3) = (0, 1)$, and indeed $g(0) = -\sqrt4 + 3 = 1$.

```plot
{"x": [-6, 6], "y": [-2, 5], "functions": [{"f": "sqrt(x)", "from": 0, "to": 6, "dashed": true, "label": "y = √x"}, {"f": "-sqrt(x + 4) + 3", "from": -4, "to": 6, "label": "g(x) = −√(x + 4) + 3"}], "points": [{"at": [-4, 3], "label": "(−4, 3)"}, {"at": [0, 1], "label": "(0, 1)"}], "caption": "The endpoint moves from (0, 0) to (−4, 3), and the graph now heads downward"}
```

### Example 3

The point $(2, 5)$ is on the graph of $y = f(x)$. Find the matching point on each graph: (a) $y = 3f(x - 1) - 4$; (b) $y = f(-x)$; (c) $y = f(2x)$.

1. (a) $h = 1$, $a = 3$, $k = -4$: $(2 + 1,\; 3 \cdot 5 - 4) = (3, 11)$. Check: at $x = 3$, $3f(3 - 1) - 4 = 3f(2) - 4 = 3(5) - 4 = 11$.
2. (b) Reflect across the $y$-axis: $(-2, 5)$, since $f(-(-2)) = f(2) = 5$.
3. (c) Horizontal compression by $\tfrac12$: $(1, 5)$, since $f(2 \cdot 1) = f(2) = 5$.

In each case you can check the answer by plugging the new $x$ into the new formula and seeing that the inside lands on the old input, 2.

## Common mistakes

- Shifting the wrong way: $y = (x + 5)^2$ moves $y = x^2$ *left* 5, not right. Ask "what input makes the inside zero?"
- Mixing up $-f(x)$ (flip top to bottom) and $f(-x)$ (flip left to right).
- Adding $k$ before multiplying by $a$. For $y = 2f(x) + 1$, a point at height 3 goes to $2(3) + 1 = 7$, not $2(3 + 1) = 8$.
- Treating $f(2x)$ as a horizontal stretch. Multiplying the input by 2 squeezes the graph toward the $y$-axis.
- Forgetting that shifts change the domain or range: $y = \sqrt{x - 2}$ has domain $x \ge 2$, and $y = x^2 - 6$ has range $y \ge -6$.

## Key points

- Learn the parent graphs: $x$, $x^2$, $x^3$, $\lvert x \rvert$, $\sqrt x$, $\sqrt[3]x$, $\tfrac1x$, $2^x$.
- $f(x) + k$: up $k$. $f(x - h)$: right $h$. Inside changes act on $x$ in the opposite way to how they look.
- $-f(x)$ reflects across the $x$-axis; $f(-x)$ reflects across the $y$-axis.
- $a f(x)$ stretches vertically by $|a|$; $f(bx)$ compresses horizontally by $\tfrac1b$.
- For $y = a f(x - h) + k$, points move $(x, y) \to (x + h, ay + k)$, and the parent's anchor point lands at $(h, k)$.

lessons.title: Piecewise-defined functions
lessons.body:
Many real rules change partway through. A phone plan charges one price up to a data cap and another price after it; a tax rate jumps at an income threshold; a parking garage charges by the started hour. A single formula can't describe these, but a function is allowed to use different formulas on different parts of its domain. This lesson shows how to read, evaluate and graph such functions, and explains two important examples: absolute value and step functions.

## What a piecewise function is

A **[[piecewise-defined function]]** (or piecewise function) uses different formulas on different intervals of its domain. It's written with a brace, each formula paired with the condition that says when to use it:

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 2x + 3 & \text{if } x < -1 \\ x^2 & \text{if } -1 \le x \le 2 \\ 5 - x & \text{if } x > 2 \end{cases}$$

The conditions must not overlap, because a function gives each input exactly one output. Each input belongs to exactly one piece, and only that piece's formula is used for it. The numbers where the rule changes, here $-1$ and $2$, are the **[[break points]]**. Pay close attention to which piece owns each break point: the symbols $<$, $\le$, $>$ and $\ge$ decide it.

## Evaluating

To find $f(a)$:

1. Find the condition that $a$ satisfies.
2. Substitute $a$ into that piece's formula only.

### Example 1

For the function $f$ above, find $f(-3)$, $f(-1)$, $f(2)$ and $f(5)$.

1. $-3 < -1$, so use the first piece: $f(-3) = 2(-3) + 3 = -3$.
2. $-1$ satisfies $-1 \le x \le 2$ (not $x < -1$), so use the second: $f(-1) = (-1)^2 = 1$.
3. $2$ also satisfies $-1 \le x \le 2$: $f(2) = 2^2 = 4$. (Using the third piece would give $5 - 2 = 3$, which is wrong because 2 is not greater than 2.)
4. $5 > 2$: $f(5) = 5 - 5 = 0$.

## Graphing

Graph each piece as if it were a whole function, but keep only the part over its own interval. At each break point, draw a closed dot if the piece includes that endpoint ($\le$ or $\ge$) and an open dot if it doesn't ($<$ or $>$).

For the function $f$ above:

- The line $y = 2x + 3$ is drawn for $x < -1$. At $x = -1$ it would reach $2(-1) + 3 = 1$, so it ends with an open dot at $(-1, 1)$.
- The parabola $y = x^2$ runs from $(-1, 1)$ to $(2, 4)$, closed at both ends. Its closed dot at $(-1, 1)$ fills in the open dot of the first piece, so the graph is unbroken there.
- The line $y = 5 - x$ is drawn for $x > 2$, starting with an open dot at $(2, 3)$.

```plot
{"x": [-5, 6], "y": [-5, 6], "functions": [{"f": "2x + 3", "from": -5, "to": -1}, {"f": "x^2", "from": -1, "to": 2}, {"f": "5 - x", "from": 2, "to": 6}], "points": [{"at": [-1, 1], "label": "(−1, 1)"}, {"at": [2, 4], "label": "(2, 4)"}, {"at": [2, 3], "open": true, "label": "(2, 3)"}], "caption": "The pieces join at x = −1, but there is a jump at x = 2: f(2) = 4, and the open dot at (2, 3) is not on the graph"}
```

At $x = 2$ the graph has a jump: the second piece ends at height 4 and the third starts at height 3. You can test any break point this way: evaluate both neighboring formulas there. If they agree, the pieces meet; if not, the graph jumps. For instance, $g(x) = x + k$ for $x < 2$ and $g(x) = x^2$ for $x \ge 2$ meet only if $2 + k = 2^2$, that is, $k = 2$.

## Absolute value as a piecewise function

The absolute value function is really a two-piece function:

$$\lvert x \rvert = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0 \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0 \end{cases}$$

The second piece looks odd at first, but if $x$ is negative then $-x$ is positive; for example $\lvert -4 \rvert = -(-4) = 4$. This is why the graph of $y = \lvert x \rvert$ is two rays: $y = x$ on the right and $y = -x$ on the left. The same idea rewrites any absolute value of a linear expression: the break point is where the inside equals zero.

### Example 2

Write $g(x) = \lvert 2x - 6 \rvert$ as a piecewise function and graph it.

1. The inside $2x - 6$ is zero at $x = 3$; it's nonnegative when $x \ge 3$ and negative when $x < 3$.
2. When $x \ge 3$, the absolute value does nothing: $g(x) = 2x - 6$.
3. When $x < 3$, it changes the sign: $g(x) = -(2x - 6) = 6 - 2x$.
4. So
$$g(x) = \begin{cases} 2x - 6 & \text{if } x \ge 3 \\ 6 - 2x & \text{if } x < 3 \end{cases}$$
5. Check: $g(1) = 6 - 2 = 4$, and $\lvert 2(1) - 6 \rvert = \lvert -4 \rvert = 4$. The graph is a V with its corner at $(3, 0)$ and slopes $\pm 2$, which is $y = \lvert x \rvert$ shifted right 3 and stretched vertically by 2, since $\lvert 2x - 6 \rvert = 2\lvert x - 3 \rvert$.

```plot
{"x": [-1, 7], "y": [-1, 8], "functions": [{"f": "6 - 2x", "from": -1, "to": 3, "label": "y = 6 − 2x"}, {"f": "2x - 6", "from": 3, "to": 7, "dashed": true, "label": "y = 2x − 6"}], "points": [{"at": [3, 0], "label": "(3, 0)"}, {"at": [1, 4], "label": "(1, 4)"}], "caption": "|2x − 6| is made of two rays that meet at (3, 0)"}
```

## Step functions

A **[[step function]]** is a piecewise function that is constant on each piece, so its graph looks like a staircase of horizontal segments. The standard example is the **[[greatest integer function]]**, also called the floor function:

$$\lfloor x \rfloor = \text{the greatest integer that is less than or equal to } x.$$

So $\lfloor 3.7 \rfloor = 3$, $\lfloor 5 \rfloor = 5$, and $\lfloor -1.2 \rfloor = -2$. That last one catches people: $-1$ is greater than $-1.2$, so the greatest integer that does not exceed $-1.2$ is $-2$. Think "round down on the number line," never "chop off the decimals."

On each interval $n \le x < n + 1$ the value is the integer $n$. Each step has a closed dot on its left end and an open dot on its right end.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 4], "y": [-3, 4], "segments": [{"from": [-3, -3], "to": [-2, -3]}, {"from": [-2, -2], "to": [-1, -2]}, {"from": [-1, -1], "to": [0, -1]}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [1, 0]}, {"from": [1, 1], "to": [2, 1]}, {"from": [2, 2], "to": [3, 2]}, {"from": [3, 3], "to": [4, 3]}], "points": [{"at": [-2, -2]}, {"at": [-1, -1]}, {"at": [0, 0]}, {"at": [1, 1]}, {"at": [2, 2]}, {"at": [3, 3]}, {"at": [-2, -3], "open": true}, {"at": [-1, -2], "open": true}, {"at": [0, -1], "open": true}, {"at": [1, 0], "open": true}, {"at": [2, 1], "open": true}, {"at": [3, 2], "open": true}], "caption": "y = ⌊x⌋: each step includes its left end and excludes its right end"}
```

Real prices that charge "per hour or part of an hour" are step functions that round up instead of down. Rather than memorize a formula, write the cases out.

### Example 3

A parking garage charges \$4 for the first hour or less and \$3 for each additional hour or part of an hour, up to a daily maximum of \$15. Write the cost $C(t)$ for $0 < t \le 24$ hours, and find the cost of parking for 2 hours, for 2 hours 10 minutes, and for 6 hours.

1. Up to 1 hour costs 4. Any time past 1 hour, up to 2, adds one more charge: 7. Past 2 hours, up to 3: 10. Past 3, up to 4: 13. Past 4 hours, the next charge would make 16, but the maximum caps it at 15.
2. As a piecewise function:
$$C(t) = \begin{cases} 4 & \text{if } 0 < t \le 1 \\ 7 & \text{if } 1 < t \le 2 \\ 10 & \text{if } 2 < t \le 3 \\ 13 & \text{if } 3 < t \le 4 \\ 15 & \text{if } 4 < t \le 24 \end{cases}$$
3. $t = 2$ is in $1 < t \le 2$, so $C(2) = 7$ dollars.
4. 2 hours 10 minutes is $t \approx 2.17$, in $2 < t \le 3$: \$10. The extra 10 minutes counts as a whole started hour.
5. $t = 6$ is in the last piece: \$15.

Because the charge rounds *up*, each step here is open on the left and closed on the right, the reverse of the floor function.

```plot
{"x": [0, 6], "y": [0, 17], "xLabel": "hours parked", "yLabel": "cost ($)", "segments": [{"from": [0, 4], "to": [1, 4]}, {"from": [1, 7], "to": [2, 7]}, {"from": [2, 10], "to": [3, 10]}, {"from": [3, 13], "to": [4, 13]}, {"from": [4, 15], "to": [6, 15]}], "points": [{"at": [0, 4], "open": true}, {"at": [1, 4]}, {"at": [1, 7], "open": true}, {"at": [2, 7]}, {"at": [2, 10], "open": true}, {"at": [3, 10]}, {"at": [3, 13], "open": true}, {"at": [4, 13]}, {"at": [4, 15], "open": true}], "caption": "The parking cost C(t): a step function that rounds up to the next started hour"}
```

## Common mistakes

- Using more than one piece for a single input, or the wrong piece at a break point. Read the inequality: at $x = 2$, "$x > 2$" does not apply.
- Drawing every piece across the whole graph instead of only over its own interval.
- Getting open and closed dots backwards. Closed means the endpoint is included ($\le$, $\ge$).
- Evaluating $\lfloor -1.2 \rfloor$ as $-1$. The floor of a negative non-integer is the next integer *down*.
- Writing $\lvert 2x - 6 \rvert$ as $2x - 6$ for $x \ge 0$. The break point is where the inside is zero ($x = 3$), not $x = 0$.

## Key points

- A piecewise function uses different formulas on non-overlapping intervals; each input uses exactly one formula.
- To evaluate, find the condition the input satisfies, then use only that formula.
- To graph, draw each piece on its interval with closed dots for included endpoints and open dots for excluded ones. Compare the neighboring formulas at a break point to see whether the graph joins or jumps.
- $\lvert x \rvert$ is $x$ for $x \ge 0$ and $-x$ for $x < 0$; for $\lvert mx + b \rvert$, the break point is where $mx + b = 0$.
- Step functions are constant on each piece. $\lfloor x \rfloor$ is the greatest integer $\le x$ (round down on the number line).

lessons.title: Combining and composing functions
lessons.body:
Functions can be built from other functions. Two can be added or multiplied output by output, the way profit is revenue minus cost. More interesting, one function's output can be fed into another, the way a price goes through a discount and then a sales tax. That second operation, composition, is the main subject of this lesson. It's also the key to the next lesson, because an inverse function is defined by what happens when you compose it with the original.

## Sum, difference, product and quotient

For two functions $f$ and $g$, define new functions by combining their outputs at each input:

| Operation | Definition |
|---|---|
| Sum | $(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$ |
| Difference | $(f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x)$ |
| Product | $(fg)(x) = f(x) \cdot g(x)$ |
| Quotient | $\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}$, where $g(x) \ne 0$ |

An input is only allowed if both $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ exist, so the domain of each new function is the overlap of the two domains. The quotient also excludes every $x$ where $g(x) = 0$.

### Example 1

Let $f(x) = x^2 - 4$ and $g(x) = x + 2$. Find $f + g$, $f - g$, $fg$ and $\dfrac fg$, with any domain restrictions.

1. Sum: $(x^2 - 4) + (x + 2) = x^2 + x - 2$.
2. Difference: $(x^2 - 4) - (x + 2) = x^2 - x - 6$. The parentheses matter: the whole of $g$ is subtracted, including the $+2$.
3. Product: $(x^2 - 4)(x + 2) = x^3 + 2x^2 - 4x - 8$.
4. Quotient: $\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x + 2} = \dfrac{(x - 2)(x + 2)}{x + 2} = x - 2$, but only for $x \ne -2$, because $g(-2) = 0$.

The quotient looks like the line $y = x - 2$, but its graph has a hole at $(-2, -4)$. The domain is decided by the original functions before any simplifying.

## Composition

The **[[composition]]** of $f$ with $g$ is the function

$$(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x)).$$

Read $f \circ g$ as "$f$ of $g$" or "$f$ after $g$." The order is right to left: $g$ acts on $x$ first, and then $f$ acts on the result. Picture two machines in a row: $x$ goes into $g$, and whatever comes out goes into $f$. The new function is called a **[[composite function]]**.

```shape
{"polygons": [{"points": [[2, 0], [4, 0], [4, 1.5], [2, 1.5]]}, {"points": [[6, 0], [8, 0], [8, 1.5], [6, 1.5]]}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0.75], "to": [2, 0.75], "arrow": true}, {"from": [4, 0.75], "to": [6, 0.75], "arrow": true}, {"from": [8, 0.75], "to": [10, 0.75], "arrow": true}], "labels": [{"at": [3, 0.75], "text": "g"}, {"at": [7, 0.75], "text": "f"}, {"at": [1, 1.2], "text": "x"}, {"at": [5, 1.2], "text": "g(x)"}, {"at": [9, 1.2], "text": "f(g(x))"}]}
```

To evaluate a composition at a number, work from the inside out. To find a formula, substitute the entire expression $g(x)$ for every $x$ in $f$.

Composition is usually not commutative: $f(g(x))$ and $g(f(x))$ are generally different. With $f(x) = x^2$ and $g(x) = x + 3$, $f(g(x)) = (x + 3)^2$ (add 3, then square) but $g(f(x)) = x^2 + 3$ (square, then add 3).

### Example 2

Let $f(x) = 2x - 1$ and $g(x) = x^2 + 1$. Find $(f \circ g)(2)$, $(g \circ f)(2)$, and formulas for $f(g(x))$ and $g(f(x))$.

1. $(f \circ g)(2) = f(g(2))$. Inside first: $g(2) = 4 + 1 = 5$. Then $f(5) = 10 - 1 = 9$.
2. $(g \circ f)(2) = g(f(2))$. Inside first: $f(2) = 3$. Then $g(3) = 9 + 1 = 10$.
3. $f(g(x)) = 2(x^2 + 1) - 1 = 2x^2 + 1$. Check at $x = 2$: $2(4) + 1 = 9$. ✓
4. $g(f(x)) = (2x - 1)^2 + 1 = 4x^2 - 4x + 2$. Check at $x = 2$: $16 - 8 + 2 = 10$. ✓

Checking a formula against a value you computed directly is a quick way to catch errors.

Compositions can also be read from tables or graphs. If a table says $g(1) = 4$ and $f(4) = -2$, then $f(g(1)) = f(4) = -2$, whatever the formulas are.

### Example 3

A store is taking 20% off everything, and you also have a \$10 coupon. Let $D(x) = 0.8x$ (the discount) and $C(x) = x - 10$ (the coupon), where $x$ is a price in dollars. Which order is better for a \$50 item?

1. Discount first, then coupon: $C(D(x)) = 0.8x - 10$. At 50: $40 - 10 = 30$ dollars.
2. Coupon first, then discount: $D(C(x)) = 0.8(x - 10) = 0.8x - 8$. At 50: $0.8(40) = 32$ dollars.
3. Taking the discount first is better by \$2 for every price, since $0.8x - 10$ is always 2 less than $0.8x - 8$. The 20% applies to the coupon's \$10 if the coupon comes first, which shrinks its value to \$8.

## The domain of a composition

For $f(g(x))$ to exist, two things must be true:

1. $x$ is in the domain of $g$ (so $g(x)$ exists), and
2. $g(x)$ is in the domain of $f$ (so $f$ can accept it).

Simplifying the final formula can hide the first condition, so find the domain from these two conditions, not just from the formula you end up with.

### Example 4

Let $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 2}$ and $g(x) = \sqrt{x}$. Find $f(g(x))$ and its domain.

1. Formula: $f(g(x)) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x} - 2}$.
2. Condition 1: $g(x) = \sqrt x$ needs $x \ge 0$.
3. Condition 2: $f$ can't accept 2, so we need $\sqrt x \ne 2$, which means $x \ne 4$.
4. Domain: $x \ge 0$ and $x \ne 4$, or in interval notation $[0, 4) \cup (4, \infty)$.

Compare $g(f(x)) = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{x - 2}}$, which needs $x \ne 2$ and $\dfrac{1}{x - 2} \ge 0$. A fraction with numerator 1 is positive exactly when its denominator is positive, so the domain is $x > 2$.

## Decomposing a function

Going the other way, you can **[[decompose]]** a complicated function: write it as $f(g(x))$ with simpler pieces. Look for an "inside" expression that the formula does something to. For $h(x) = (3x + 1)^5$, the inside is $3x + 1$ and the outside action is "raise to the 5th power," so $g(x) = 3x + 1$ and $f(x) = x^5$. For $h(x) = \sqrt{x^2 + 9}$, take $g(x) = x^2 + 9$ and $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$.

Decompositions aren't unique ($h(x) = (3x + 1)^5$ is also $f(g(x))$ with $g(x) = 3x$ and $f(x) = (x + 1)^5$), but the natural choice is usually the inside expression. This skill becomes essential in calculus, where the chain rule differentiates composite functions.

## Common mistakes

- Doing the composition in the wrong order. In $f(g(x))$, $g$ goes first, even though $f$ is written first.
- Multiplying instead of composing: $f(g(x))$ is not $f(x) \cdot g(x)$.
- Substituting $g(x)$ for only one of the $x$'s in $f$. Every $x$ gets replaced.
- Forgetting parentheses when subtracting or squaring: $(f - g)(x) = x^2 - 4 - (x + 2)$, and $f(2x - 1)$ with $f(x) = x^2$ is $(2x - 1)^2$, not $2x^2 - 1$.
- Finding the domain from the simplified formula alone. Restrictions from the inner function, or from a cancelled factor in a quotient, still apply.

## Key points

- $f + g$, $f - g$, $fg$ and $\tfrac fg$ combine outputs; their domain is where both $f$ and $g$ are defined, and $\tfrac fg$ also needs $g(x) \ne 0$.
- $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$: apply $g$ first, then $f$. Evaluate from the inside out.
- Usually $f(g(x)) \ne g(f(x))$.
- The domain of $f \circ g$: $x$ must be in the domain of $g$, and $g(x)$ must be in the domain of $f$.
- Decompose by spotting an inside expression $g(x)$ and an outside action $f$.

lessons.title: Inverse functions
lessons.body:
A function turns inputs into outputs. Often you want to go backward: given a temperature in Fahrenheit, what was it in Celsius? Given the balance in an account, how long has it been growing? An inverse function runs a function in reverse. This lesson explains when an inverse exists, how to find one, what its graph looks like, and how to use composition from the last lesson to check that you have the right one. Inverses come back in Module 6, where the logarithm is defined as the inverse of an exponential function.

## Undoing a function

If $f$ sends $a$ to $b$, its inverse sends $b$ back to $a$:

$$f(a) = b \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f^{-1}(b) = a.$$

The notation $f^{-1}$ is read "$f$ inverse." The $-1$ is not an exponent here: $f^{-1}(x)$ does not mean $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$.

Because inputs and outputs trade places, every point $(a, b)$ on $f$ becomes the point $(b, a)$ on $f^{-1}$, and the domain and range swap: the domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, and the range of $f^{-1}$ is the domain of $f$. With a table, you can find the inverse by swapping the columns:

| $x$ | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $f(x)$ | 5 | 7 | 9 | 11 |

So $f^{-1}(9) = 2$ and $f^{-1}(5) = 0$.

## When does an inverse exist?

Running a function backward only works if each output came from just one input. A function is **[[one-to-one]]** if different inputs always give different outputs: $f(a) = f(b)$ only when $a = b$.

The squaring function is not one-to-one, since $f(3) = f(-3) = 9$. Asked "which input gave 9?", there's no single answer, so $y = x^2$ has no inverse function on all the real numbers.

The **[[horizontal line test]]** checks this with a graph: a function is one-to-one exactly when no horizontal line crosses its graph more than once. (A horizontal line at height $b$ meets the graph at every input whose output is $b$.) Compare the vertical line test from Algebra 1, which decides whether a graph is a function at all.

When a function fails the test, you can often **[[restrict the domain]]** to a part where it passes. Keeping only $x \ge 0$ makes $y = x^2$ one-to-one, and its inverse on that piece is $y = \sqrt{x}$. That's exactly why $\sqrt x$ means the nonnegative root.

A function with an inverse is called **[[invertible]]**, and its inverse is the **[[inverse function]]**: the function $f^{-1}$ with $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$ for every $x$ in the domain of $f$ and $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$ for every $x$ in the domain of $f^{-1}$.

## Finding an inverse algebraically

1. Replace $f(x)$ with $y$.
2. Swap $x$ and $y$. (This is the "trade inputs and outputs" step.)
3. Solve the new equation for $y$.
4. Replace $y$ with $f^{-1}(x)$, and state its domain (the range of $f$) if it's restricted.

### Example 1

Find the inverse of $f(x) = 3x - 5$ and verify it by composition.

1. $y = 3x - 5$.
2. Swap: $x = 3y - 5$.
3. Solve: $x + 5 = 3y$, so $y = \dfrac{x + 5}{3}$.
4. $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x + 5}{3}$.

This makes sense as a reversal: $f$ multiplies by 3 and then subtracts 5, and $f^{-1}$ undoes those steps in reverse order, adding 5 and then dividing by 3.

Verify: $f(f^{-1}(x)) = 3\left(\dfrac{x + 5}{3}\right) - 5 = x + 5 - 5 = x$, and $f^{-1}(f(x)) = \dfrac{(3x - 5) + 5}{3} = \dfrac{3x}{3} = x$. Both compositions give $x$, so the inverse is correct.

### Example 2

Find the inverse of $f(x) = \sqrt{x - 2}$, then graph both.

1. The domain of $f$ is $x \ge 2$ and its range is $y \ge 0$. It passes the horizontal line test, since it always increases.
2. $y = \sqrt{x - 2}$. Swap: $x = \sqrt{y - 2}$.
3. Square both sides: $x^2 = y - 2$, so $y = x^2 + 2$.
4. The domain of $f^{-1}$ is the range of $f$, so $f^{-1}(x) = x^2 + 2$ **for $x \ge 0$** only. Without that restriction, $x^2 + 2$ would be a whole parabola, which isn't one-to-one.

Check one point: $f(6) = \sqrt4 = 2$, and $f^{-1}(2) = 4 + 2 = 6$. ✓

## The graph of an inverse

Since $(a, b)$ on $f$ becomes $(b, a)$ on $f^{-1}$, and swapping coordinates is the same as reflecting across the line $y = x$, the graph of $f^{-1}$ is the mirror image of the graph of $f$ across $y = x$.

```plot
{"x": [-1, 8], "y": [-1, 8], "equal": true, "functions": [{"f": "sqrt(x - 2)", "from": 2, "to": 8, "label": "f(x) = √(x − 2)"}, {"f": "x^2 + 2", "from": 0, "to": 2.45, "dashed": true, "label": "f⁻¹(x) = x² + 2, x ≥ 0"}, {"f": "x", "from": -1, "to": 8, "color": "gray", "label": "y = x"}], "points": [{"at": [6, 2], "label": "(6, 2)"}, {"at": [2, 6], "label": "(2, 6)"}, {"at": [2, 0]}, {"at": [0, 2]}], "caption": "A function and its inverse are reflections of each other across y = x"}
```

You can use this to sketch an inverse without a formula: reflect a few key points and connect them.

### Example 3

Find the inverse of $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}$.

1. $y = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}$. Swap: $x = \dfrac{2y + 1}{y - 3}$.
2. Clear the fraction: $x(y - 3) = 2y + 1$, so $xy - 3x = 2y + 1$.
3. Collect the $y$ terms on one side and factor out $y$: $xy - 2y = 3x + 1$, so $y(x - 2) = 3x + 1$.
4. $f^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{3x + 1}{x - 2}$.

The domain of $f$ excludes 3, and the domain of $f^{-1}$ excludes 2. That fits: $f$ never outputs 2 (its horizontal asymptote, which Module 5 explains), so 2 is not in the range of $f$. Check: $f(4) = \dfrac{9}{1} = 9$ and $f^{-1}(9) = \dfrac{28}{7} = 4$. ✓

### Example 4

Is $g(x) = x^2 - 4x$ one-to-one? If not, restrict its domain to $x \ge 2$ and find the inverse there.

1. $g(0) = 0$ and $g(4) = 16 - 16 = 0$: two inputs, same output. Not one-to-one.
2. Complete the square: $g(x) = (x - 2)^2 - 4$. It's a parabola with vertex $(2, -4)$, so on $x \ge 2$ it rises and passes the horizontal line test. Its range there is $y \ge -4$.
3. Swap: $x = (y - 2)^2 - 4$. Then $x + 4 = (y - 2)^2$.
4. Take the square root. On this piece $y \ge 2$, so $y - 2 \ge 0$ and we take the positive root: $y - 2 = \sqrt{x + 4}$.
5. $g^{-1}(x) = 2 + \sqrt{x + 4}$, with domain $x \ge -4$. Check: $g(5) = 25 - 20 = 5$, and $g^{-1}(5) = 2 + \sqrt9 = 5$. ✓

## Common mistakes

- Reading $f^{-1}(x)$ as $\dfrac{1}{f(x)}$. The inverse undoes $f$; the reciprocal divides 1 by it.
- Undoing the steps in the original order. Undo the last step first: the inverse of "times 3, then minus 5" is "plus 5, then divide by 3," not "divide by 3, then plus 5."
- Forgetting to restrict the domain of the inverse to the range of $f$, as in $f^{-1}(x) = x^2 + 2$ for $x \ge 0$.
- Claiming an inverse for a function that isn't one-to-one, such as $y = x^2$ on all real numbers.
- Checking only one composition. For a full check, $f(f^{-1}(x))$ and $f^{-1}(f(x))$ should both simplify to $x$.

## Key points

- $f(a) = b$ means $f^{-1}(b) = a$; points $(a, b)$ become $(b, a)$, and the domain and range swap.
- An inverse function exists exactly when $f$ is one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test). Restrict the domain if necessary.
- To find $f^{-1}$: write $y = f(x)$, swap $x$ and $y$, solve for $y$.
- The graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ across $y = x$.
- Verify with composition: $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$ and $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$.

lessons.title: Complex numbers
lessons.body:
Some quadratic equations, like $x^2 + 1 = 0$, have no real solutions, because no real number squares to a negative. Mathematicians enlarged the number system by inventing a number whose square is $-1$. The result, the complex numbers, gives every quadratic equation solutions, and it's essential in later mathematics, physics and engineering. This lesson defines complex numbers and shows how to compute with them.

## The imaginary unit

The **[[imaginary unit]]** $i$ is defined by

$$i^2 = -1, \qquad \text{so } i = \sqrt{-1}.$$

With it, square roots of negative numbers make sense: for $b > 0$, $\sqrt{-b} = i\sqrt{b}$. So $\sqrt{-16} = 4i$ and $\sqrt{-12} = i\sqrt{12} = 2i\sqrt3$.

Always rewrite $\sqrt{-b}$ as $i\sqrt b$ before multiplying. The rule $\sqrt a\sqrt b = \sqrt{ab}$ is false when both are negative: $\sqrt{-4}\sqrt{-9} = (2i)(3i) = 6i^2 = -6$, not $\sqrt{36} = 6$.

## Complex numbers

A **[[complex number]]** has the form $a + bi$ with $a$ and $b$ real. Its **[[real part]]** is $a$ and its **[[imaginary part]]** is $b$ (the number $b$, not $bi$). If $b = 0$ it's a real number; if $a = 0$ and $b \ne 0$, it's a **[[pure imaginary number]]**, like $3i$. Two complex numbers are equal exactly when their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal.

Complex numbers can be pictured as points in the **[[complex plane]]**: $a + bi$ sits at $(a, b)$, with real parts along the horizontal axis and imaginary parts along the vertical axis.

```plot
{"x": [-5, 5], "y": [-4, 4], "equal": true, "xLabel": "real", "yLabel": "imaginary", "points": [{"at": [3, 2], "label": "3 + 2i"}, {"at": [3, -2], "label": "3 - 2i"}, {"at": [-2, 3], "label": "-2 + 3i"}, {"at": [0, -3], "label": "-3i"}, {"at": [4, 0], "label": "4"}], "segments": [{"from": [0, 0], "to": [3, 2], "arrow": true}, {"from": [0, 0], "to": [3, -2], "arrow": true, "dashed": true}], "caption": "The complex plane; a number and its conjugate are mirror images across the real axis"}
```

## Adding, subtracting and multiplying

Treat $i$ like a variable, then replace $i^2$ by $-1$.

- Add or subtract real parts and imaginary parts separately: $(3 + 2i) + (1 - 5i) = 4 - 3i$.
- Multiply with the distributive property (FOIL), then use $i^2 = -1$.

### Example 1

Compute $(2 + 3i)(4 - i)$.

1. FOIL: $8 - 2i + 12i - 3i^2$.
2. Replace $i^2$: $-3i^2 = -3(-1) = 3$.
3. Combine: $8 + 3 + 10i = 11 + 10i$.

## The conjugate and division

The **[[complex conjugate]]** of $a + bi$ is $a - bi$. Their product is always a nonnegative real number:

$$(a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 - b^2i^2 = a^2 + b^2.$$

That's the key to division, which works like rationalizing a denominator: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.

### Example 2

Write $\dfrac{5 + i}{2 - 3i}$ in the form $a + bi$.

1. Multiply by $\dfrac{2 + 3i}{2 + 3i}$.
2. Numerator: $(5 + i)(2 + 3i) = 10 + 15i + 2i + 3i^2 = 7 + 17i$.
3. Denominator: $2^2 + 3^2 = 13$.
4. Result: $\dfrac{7}{13} + \dfrac{17}{13}i$.

## Powers of $i$

The powers of $i$ repeat in a cycle of four:

| $i^1$ | $i^2$ | $i^3$ | $i^4$ | $i^5$ | $i^6$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $i$ | $-1$ | $-i$ | $1$ | $i$ | $-1$ |

Since $i^4 = 1$, divide the exponent by 4 and keep the remainder: $i^{n} = i^{r}$ where $r$ is the remainder of $n \div 4$ (with $i^0 = 1$). For example, $i^{43}$: $43 = 4 \cdot 10 + 3$, so $i^{43} = i^3 = -i$.

## Complex solutions of quadratic equations

With complex numbers, the quadratic formula always gives two solutions (counting a double root twice). When the discriminant is negative, they are complex conjugates of each other. Here are a few first examples; the next lesson treats these quadratics in detail.

### Example 3

Solve $x^2 - 4x + 13 = 0$.

1. $D = 16 - 52 = -36$, so $\sqrt{D} = \sqrt{-36} = 6i$.
2. $x = \dfrac{4 \pm 6i}{2} = 2 \pm 3i$.
3. Check $x = 2 + 3i$: $(2 + 3i)^2 = 4 + 12i - 9 = -5 + 12i$. Then $-5 + 12i - 4(2 + 3i) + 13 = -5 + 12i - 8 - 12i + 13 = 0$.

### Example 4

Solve $(x + 1)^2 = -9$.

$x + 1 = \pm 3i$, so $x = -1 \pm 3i$. (With real numbers only, as in Algebra 1, this equation had no solution, since a square can't be negative; now it has two complex ones.)

This also completes a fact from Algebra 1: a sum of squares such as $x^2 + 9$ can't be factored using real numbers, but it does factor over the complex numbers: $x^2 + 9 = (x + 3i)(x - 3i)$.

### Example 5

Simplify $(2 - i)^2 + \dfrac{3 + 4i}{i}$.

1. Square: $(2 - i)^2 = 4 - 4i + i^2 = 3 - 4i$.
2. Divide by $i$: multiply top and bottom by $-i$ (the conjugate of $i$): $\dfrac{(3 + 4i)(-i)}{i(-i)} = \dfrac{-3i - 4i^2}{1} = 4 - 3i$.
3. Add: $(3 - 4i) + (4 - 3i) = 7 - 7i$.

The conjugate of $i = 0 + 1i$ is $-i$, and $i(-i) = -i^2 = 1$, which is why dividing by $i$ is the same as multiplying by $-i$.

## Common mistakes

- Writing $\sqrt{-4}\sqrt{-9} = \sqrt{36}$. Convert to $i$ first.
- Forgetting that $i^2 = -1$ after FOIL, leaving answers like $8 + 10i - 3i^2$.
- Multiplying by the conjugate of the numerator instead of the denominator when dividing.
- Calling the imaginary part of $4 - 7i$ "$-7i$"; it's $-7$.
- Thinking $-36$ has no square root at all. It has no real square root; its square roots are $\pm 6i$.

## Key points

- $i^2 = -1$; for $b > 0$, $\sqrt{-b} = i\sqrt b$.
- Complex numbers $a + bi$ add and multiply like binomials, with $i^2$ replaced by $-1$.
- $(a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 + b^2$; divide by multiplying top and bottom by the denominator's conjugate.
- Powers of $i$ cycle with period 4: $i, -1, -i, 1$.
- A quadratic with negative discriminant has two complex conjugate solutions.

lessons.title: Quadratics with complex solutions
lessons.body:
In Algebra 1, some quadratic equations had "no solution" because the parabola never touched the $x$-axis. The last lesson gave those equations solutions: complex numbers. This lesson puts the two ideas together. You'll see how the graph tells you in advance whether the solutions are real or complex, solve such equations by completing the square and by the quadratic formula, see why complex solutions always come as a conjugate pair, and run the process backward to build a quadratic with given roots.

## Vertex form and what the graph says

Recall from Algebra 1 that a quadratic written in **[[vertex form]]**,

$$f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k,$$

has its vertex at $(h, k)$ and opens up if $a > 0$, down if $a < 0$. (In the language of Module 1, it's $y = x^2$ stretched by $a$ and shifted so the vertex lands at $(h, k)$.) You get vertex form from $ax^2 + bx + c$ by **[[completing the square]]**: add and subtract the square of half the $x$-coefficient so that part of the expression becomes a perfect square.

Vertex form makes the equation $f(x) = 0$ easy to solve:

$$a(x - h)^2 + k = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; (x - h)^2 = -\frac{k}{a} \;\Longrightarrow\; x = h \pm \sqrt{-\frac{k}{a}}.$$

If $-\tfrac ka$ is negative, the square root is imaginary and the solutions are complex. That happens exactly when $a$ and $k$ have the same sign, and the graph shows why: a parabola that opens up with its vertex above the $x$-axis (or opens down with its vertex below it) never crosses the axis, so there are no real zeros.

### Example 1

Solve $x^2 + 6x + 13 = 0$ by completing the square, and explain the answer with the graph.

1. Half of 6 is 3, and $3^2 = 9$: $x^2 + 6x + 13 = (x^2 + 6x + 9) + 4 = (x + 3)^2 + 4$.
2. Set it to zero: $(x + 3)^2 = -4$.
3. Take square roots: $x + 3 = \pm\sqrt{-4} = \pm 2i$.
4. $x = -3 \pm 2i$.
5. Check $x = -3 + 2i$: $(2i)^2 + 4 = -4 + 4 = 0$. ✓

The graph of $y = (x + 3)^2 + 4$ opens up from the vertex $(-3, 4)$, which is above the $x$-axis, so it has no $x$-intercepts. Notice that the real part of the solutions, $-3$, is the $x$-coordinate of the vertex.

```plot
{"x": [-7, 2], "y": [-1, 10], "functions": [{"f": "x^2 + 6x + 13", "label": "y = x² + 6x + 13"}], "points": [{"at": [-3, 4], "label": "vertex (−3, 4)"}], "segments": [{"from": [-3, -1], "to": [-3, 10], "dashed": true}], "caption": "The parabola never reaches the x-axis, so its zeros −3 ± 2i are not real; their real part is the axis of symmetry x = −3"}
```

## The discriminant decides

For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, the **[[quadratic formula]]** gives

$$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}.$$

The quantity under the root, $b^2 - 4ac$, is the **[[discriminant]]**. Its sign tells you what kind of solutions to expect before you finish the work:

| Discriminant | Solutions | Graph of $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ |
|---|---|---|
| $b^2 - 4ac > 0$ | two different real solutions | crosses the $x$-axis twice |
| $b^2 - 4ac = 0$ | one real **[[double root]]** | touches the $x$-axis at the vertex |
| $b^2 - 4ac < 0$ | two non-real complex solutions, conjugates of each other | never meets the $x$-axis |

So "no real solution" never means "no solution" anymore. Every quadratic equation has exactly two solutions in the complex numbers, if a double root is counted twice.

When the discriminant is negative, write $\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} = i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}$, simplify the radical, and then divide *both* terms of the numerator by $2a$ to get the form $p \pm qi$.

### Example 2

Solve $2x^2 - 4x + 5 = 0$.

1. $a = 2$, $b = -4$, $c = 5$. Discriminant: $(-4)^2 - 4(2)(5) = 16 - 40 = -24$.
2. $\sqrt{-24} = i\sqrt{24} = i\sqrt{4 \cdot 6} = 2i\sqrt6$.
3. $x = \dfrac{4 \pm 2i\sqrt6}{4}$.
4. Split the fraction and reduce each part: $x = \dfrac44 \pm \dfrac{2\sqrt6}{4}i = 1 \pm \dfrac{\sqrt6}{2}i$.

A common slip in step 4 is to divide only the 4 by 4 and write $1 \pm 2i\sqrt6$.

### Example 3

Solve $-2(x - 1)^2 - 8 = 0$ without expanding.

1. Here $a = -2$ and $k = -8$ have the same sign, so expect complex solutions (the parabola opens down from $(1, -8)$, below the axis).
2. $-2(x - 1)^2 = 8$, so $(x - 1)^2 = -4$.
3. $x - 1 = \pm 2i$, so $x = 1 \pm 2i$.

## Why the solutions are conjugates

When the discriminant $D$ is negative, the formula splits into a real part and an imaginary part:

$$x = -\frac{b}{2a} \pm \frac{\sqrt{-D}}{2a}\,i.$$

Both solutions have the same real part, $-\tfrac{b}{2a}$ (the $x$-coordinate of the vertex), and opposite imaginary parts. They are a **[[conjugate pair]]**, $p + qi$ and $p - qi$. So if the coefficients are real and you know one complex solution, you know the other: if $4 - i$ is a solution, so is $4 + i$.

Two more facts help check answers. For any quadratic $ax^2 + bx + c$ with solutions $r$ and $s$:

$$r + s = -\frac{b}{a}, \qquad rs = \frac{c}{a}.$$

In Example 2, the sum is $\left(1 + \tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}i\right) + \left(1 - \tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}i\right) = 2 = -\tfrac{-4}{2}$, and the product is $1^2 + \left(\tfrac{\sqrt6}{2}\right)^2 = 1 + \tfrac64 = \tfrac52 = \tfrac{c}{a}$. Both match. (The product uses $(p + qi)(p - qi) = p^2 + q^2$ from the last lesson.)

## Writing a quadratic from its roots

If $r$ and $s$ are the roots, then $(x - r)(x - s)$ is a quadratic with exactly those roots, by the zero product property; any multiple $a(x - r)(x - s)$ works too. With a conjugate pair $p \pm qi$, the product simplifies nicely if you group the real part with $x$:

$$\big(x - (p + qi)\big)\big(x - (p - qi)\big) = \big((x - p) - qi\big)\big((x - p) + qi\big) = (x - p)^2 + q^2.$$

This is a difference of squares in which $-(qi)^2 = q^2$. The result has real coefficients, and it's already in vertex form: vertex $(p, q^2)$.

### Example 4

Write a quadratic with leading coefficient 1 whose roots are $2 \pm 5i$.

1. $p = 2$, $q = 5$: $(x - 2)^2 + 25$.
2. Expand: $x^2 - 4x + 4 + 25 = x^2 - 4x + 29$.
3. Check with sum and product: the roots add to 4, which is $-\tfrac{-4}{1}$, and multiply to $2^2 + 5^2 = 29 = \tfrac{29}{1}$. ✓

### Example 5

A quadratic has real coefficients, leading coefficient 2, and one root $3 - i\sqrt2$. Find it.

1. The other root is the conjugate, $3 + i\sqrt2$. So $p = 3$, $q = \sqrt2$, $q^2 = 2$.
2. $2\left[(x - 3)^2 + 2\right] = 2(x^2 - 6x + 11) = 2x^2 - 12x + 22$.

## Common mistakes

- Saying a quadratic with negative discriminant has "no solution." It has no *real* solution; it has two complex ones.
- Writing $\sqrt{-24}$ as $-2\sqrt6$. The square root of a negative is imaginary: $2i\sqrt6$.
- Dividing only part of the numerator by $2a$. Both $-b$ and the root term get divided.
- Sign errors in $(x - r)$: for the root $-1 + 3i$, the factor is $x - (-1 + 3i) = x + 1 - 3i$.
- Forgetting the conjugate. A real quadratic can't have just one non-real root.

## Key points

- In vertex form $a(x - h)^2 + k = 0$, the solutions are $h \pm \sqrt{-k/a}$; they're complex when $a$ and $k$ have the same sign (the parabola misses the $x$-axis).
- Discriminant $b^2 - 4ac$: positive, two real roots; zero, a double root; negative, two complex conjugate roots.
- For a negative discriminant, $x = -\tfrac{b}{2a} \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a}i$.
- Roots $r$, $s$ of $ax^2 + bx + c$ satisfy $r + s = -\tfrac ba$ and $rs = \tfrac ca$.
- Roots $p \pm qi$ come from $(x - p)^2 + q^2$; multiply by $a$ for another leading coefficient.

lessons.title: Nonlinear systems
lessons.body:
In Algebra 1 you solved systems of two linear equations. Two different lines meet at most once, so those systems had one solution, none, or (for the same line twice) infinitely many. Once a parabola or a circle is involved, the picture changes: a line can cross a parabola twice, touch it once, or miss it completely. This lesson solves such systems with the same two methods you already know, substitution and elimination, and uses the discriminant from the last lesson to predict how many solutions there are before you find them.

## What a nonlinear system is

A **[[nonlinear system]]** is a system of equations in which at least one equation is not linear: it has a squared variable, a product like $xy$, a variable in a denominator, and so on. A solution is still an ordered pair $(x, y)$ that makes every equation true, and graphically it is still a point where the graphs meet.

Two curves you'll see often:

- a parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$;
- a **[[circle]]**. The circle with center $(0, 0)$ and radius $r$ is $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$, because by the Pythagorean theorem a point $(x, y)$ is at distance $\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$ from the origin. Moving the center to $(h, k)$ gives $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$.

The figure shows why the number of solutions varies. Each line meets the parabola $y = x^2$ a different number of times.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 4], "y": [-4, 9], "functions": [{"f": "x^2", "label": "y = x²"}, {"f": "x + 2", "label": "y = x + 2", "dashed": true}, {"f": "2*x - 1", "label": "y = 2x − 1"}, {"f": "x - 3", "label": "y = x − 3", "dashed": true}], "points": [{"at": [-1, 1], "label": "(−1, 1)"}, {"at": [2, 4], "label": "(2, 4)"}, {"at": [1, 1], "label": "(1, 1)"}], "caption": "y = x + 2 crosses twice, y = 2x − 1 touches once at (1, 1), y = x − 3 misses"}
```

## Substitution

Substitution is the workhorse, and it's the natural choice when one equation is linear.

1. Solve the linear equation (or the simpler equation) for one variable.
2. Substitute into the other equation. You get one equation in one variable, usually a quadratic.
3. Solve it. Each solution is the first coordinate of an intersection point.
4. Find the partner coordinate from the *linear* equation (or the one you solved in step 1).
5. Check each pair in both original equations.

Step 4 matters. If you go back to an equation with a square in it, such as $y^2 = 16$, you get $y = \pm 4$ and can't tell which sign belongs with which $x$. The linear equation gives exactly one partner for each $x$.

### Example 1

Solve $y = x^2 - 4x + 3$ and $y = x - 1$.

1. Both equations are already solved for $y$, so set the right sides equal: $x^2 - 4x + 3 = x - 1$.
2. Standard form: $x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0$, which factors as $(x - 1)(x - 4) = 0$. So $x = 1$ or $x = 4$.
3. Partners from the line $y = x - 1$: $x = 1$ gives $y = 0$; $x = 4$ gives $y = 3$.
4. Check in the parabola: $1 - 4 + 3 = 0$ and $16 - 16 + 3 = 3$. Both work.

The solutions are $(1, 0)$ and $(4, 3)$.

### Example 2

Solve $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ and $y = x + 1$.

1. Substitute $y = x + 1$ into the circle: $x^2 + (x + 1)^2 = 25$.
2. Expand carefully, using $(x + 1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1$: $2x^2 + 2x + 1 = 25$, so $2x^2 + 2x - 24 = 0$.
3. Divide by 2: $x^2 + x - 12 = 0$, so $(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0$ and $x = -4$ or $x = 3$.
4. Partners from $y = x + 1$: $(-4, -3)$ and $(3, 4)$.
5. Check in the circle: $16 + 9 = 25$ and $9 + 16 = 25$.

```plot
{"x": [-7, 7], "y": [-7, 7], "equal": true, "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 5}], "functions": [{"f": "x + 1", "label": "y = x + 1"}], "points": [{"at": [3, 4], "label": "(3, 4)"}, {"at": [-4, -3], "label": "(−4, −3)"}], "caption": "The line cuts the circle x² + y² = 25 at two points"}
```

## How many solutions? Use the discriminant

When substitution leaves a quadratic $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, its discriminant $D = b^2 - 4ac$ counts the intersection points, because each real root gives one point:

| Discriminant | Real roots | Graphs |
|---|---|---|
| $D > 0$ | two | the line crosses the curve twice |
| $D = 0$ | one (a double root) | the line just touches the curve (it is tangent to it) |
| $D < 0$ | none (two complex roots) | the line misses the curve |

Complex roots are perfectly good solutions of the quadratic, but they don't give points you can plot, so a system with $D < 0$ has no real solution.

### Example 3

For which values of $k$ does the line $y = 2x + k$ meet the parabola $y = x^2$?

1. Substitute: $x^2 = 2x + k$, so $x^2 - 2x - k = 0$.
2. The discriminant is $D = (-2)^2 - 4(1)(-k) = 4 + 4k$.
3. Two points when $4 + 4k > 0$, that is $k > -1$; one point when $k = -1$; none when $k < -1$.

With $k = -1$ the quadratic is $x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2 = 0$, so the line $y = 2x - 1$ touches the parabola only at $(1, 1)$, as in the first figure.

## Elimination

When both equations contain $x^2$ and $y^2$ (and no other $x$ or $y$ terms), add or subtract them to eliminate one squared variable, just as you would eliminate $x$ or $y$ in a linear system. Treat $x^2$ and $y^2$ as the unknowns.

### Example 4

Solve $x^2 + y^2 = 13$ and $x^2 - y^2 = 5$.

1. Add the equations: $2x^2 = 18$, so $x^2 = 9$.
2. Substitute into the first: $9 + y^2 = 13$, so $y^2 = 4$.
3. Now take square roots: $x = \pm 3$ and $y = \pm 2$. Here every combination works, because only $x^2$ and $y^2$ appear in the equations.

There are four solutions: $(3, 2)$, $(3, -2)$, $(-3, 2)$ and $(-3, -2)$. The second graph is a curve called a hyperbola (you'll meet it in precalculus); you don't need to know its shape to solve the system.

```plot
{"x": [-6, 6], "y": [-5, 5], "equal": true, "circles": [{"center": [0, 0], "r": 3.6056}], "curves": [{"x": "sqrt(5)*cosh(t)", "y": "sqrt(5)*sinh(t)", "t": [-1.6, 1.6], "color": "var(--fig-0)"}, {"x": "-sqrt(5)*cosh(t)", "y": "sqrt(5)*sinh(t)", "t": [-1.6, 1.6], "color": "var(--fig-0)"}], "labels": [{"at": [4.6, 1.2], "text": "x² − y² = 5"}, {"at": [2.2, 3.9], "text": "x² + y² = 13"}], "points": [{"at": [3, 2], "label": "(3, 2)"}, {"at": [3, -2], "label": "(3, −2)"}, {"at": [-3, 2], "label": "(−3, 2)"}, {"at": [-3, -2], "label": "(−3, −2)"}], "caption": "The circle x² + y² = 13 meets the hyperbola x² − y² = 5 at four points"}
```

Two quadratic curves can meet up to four times, so don't stop at two answers.

## An application

### Example 5

A rectangular garden has a perimeter of 20 m and an area of 24 m². Find its dimensions.

1. Let the length be $L$ and the width $W$. Perimeter: $2L + 2W = 20$, so $L + W = 10$. Area: $LW = 24$. The second equation is nonlinear.
2. From the first, $W = 10 - L$. Substitute: $L(10 - L) = 24$, so $L^2 - 10L + 24 = 0$.
3. Factor: $(L - 4)(L - 6) = 0$, so $L = 4$ or $L = 6$, giving $W = 6$ or $W = 4$.

Both solutions describe the same garden: 6 m by 4 m. Check: $2(6) + 2(4) = 20$ and $6 \cdot 4 = 24$.

## Common mistakes

- Finding the partner $y$ from an equation with $y^2$ in it, then listing both signs. Use the linear equation, or check every pair.
- Squaring a binomial term by term: $(x + 1)^2$ is $x^2 + 2x + 1$, not $x^2 + 1$.
- Reporting only the $x$-values. A solution of a system is an ordered pair.
- Stopping at two solutions when elimination gives $x = \pm a$ and $y = \pm b$; all four sign combinations may work.
- Treating complex roots of the substituted quadratic as intersection points. They mean the graphs don't meet.

## Key points

- A nonlinear system has at least one nonlinear equation; its real solutions are the intersection points of the graphs.
- Substitution: solve the linear equation for one variable, substitute, solve the quadratic, and get partners from the linear equation.
- After substituting, the discriminant tells how many intersection points there are: two, one (tangent) or none.
- Elimination works when both equations have only $x^2$ and $y^2$ terms; take $\pm$ square roots at the end.
- A line meets a parabola or circle at most twice; two quadratic curves can meet up to four times.

lessons.title: Systems in three variables
lessons.body:
Some problems have three unknowns: three kinds of ticket, three investments, or the three coefficients of a parabola. Three unknowns need three equations. The elimination method from Algebra 1 extends naturally: use pairs of equations to knock out one variable, which leaves an ordinary two-variable system. The next lesson redoes the same work more efficiently with matrices.

## What a solution looks like

A **[[linear equation in three variables]]** has the form $ax + by + cz = d$. A solution of a three-variable system is an **[[ordered triple]]** $(x, y, z)$ satisfying all the equations.

Geometrically, each such equation describes a flat plane in three-dimensional space. Three planes can meet in a single point (one solution), have no point common to all three (no solution), or share a whole line or plane (infinitely many solutions). The algebra tells you which case you're in, just as with two lines.

## The elimination strategy

1. Pick a variable to eliminate, preferably one with simple coefficients.
2. Use one pair of equations to eliminate it, producing equation (A) in the other two variables.
3. Use a different pair (it must include the third equation) to eliminate the same variable, producing equation (B).
4. Solve the two-variable system (A), (B).
5. Back-substitute into an original equation to find the third variable.
6. Check the triple in all three original equations.

The crucial point in step 3: eliminate the same variable both times. Otherwise (A) and (B) won't share the same two variables.

### Example 1

Solve
$$\begin{cases} x + y + z = 6 & (1) \\ 2x - y + z = 3 & (2) \\ x + 2y - z = 2 & (3) \end{cases}$$

1. Eliminate $z$, which has coefficients $\pm1$ everywhere.
2. Add (1) and (3): $2x + 3y = 8$. Call this (A).
3. Add (2) and (3): $3x + y = 5$. Call this (B).
4. Solve (A) and (B). From (B), $y = 5 - 3x$. Substitute into (A): $2x + 3(5 - 3x) = 8$, so $-7x = -7$ and $x = 1$. Then $y = 2$.
5. From (1): $1 + 2 + z = 6$, so $z = 3$.
6. Check: (2) gives $2 - 2 + 3 = 3$ and (3) gives $1 + 4 - 3 = 2$. The solution is $(1, 2, 3)$.

### Example 2

Solve
$$\begin{cases} 2x + 3y - z = 1 & (1) \\ x - 2y + 3z = 13 & (2) \\ 3x + y + 2z = 16 & (3) \end{cases}$$

1. Eliminate $x$, using (2), whose $x$-coefficient is 1.
2. (1) $- 2\times$(2): $(2x + 3y - z) - (2x - 4y + 6z) = 1 - 26$, so $7y - 7z = -25$. Call this (A).
3. (3) $- 3\times$(2): $(3x + y + 2z) - (3x - 6y + 9z) = 16 - 39$, so $7y - 7z = -23$. Call this (B).
4. (A) $-$ (B): $0 = -2$. False.

In fact, adding (1) and (2) gives $3x + y + 2z = 14$, which flatly contradicts (3). So this system has no solution: the three planes have no common point. This is the three-variable version of parallel lines. Not every system with "nice-looking" coefficients has a solution, and the elimination process reveals it.

## Special cases

As with two variables, watch what happens when variables vanish:

- a false statement such as $0 = 2$ means the system is **[[inconsistent]]**: no solution;
- a true statement such as $0 = 0$ means the equations are dependent, and (if the rest is consistent) there are infinitely many solutions.

For example, in $x + y + z = 3$, $x - y + 2z = 1$, $2x + 3z = 4$, the third equation is exactly the sum of the first two. It adds no new information, so we really have only two conditions on three unknowns, and infinitely many triples satisfy them.

## Fitting a parabola through three points

A classic use: any three points with different $x$-coordinates (not all on one line) lie on exactly one parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$. Substituting each point gives one linear equation in $a$, $b$, $c$.

### Example 3

Find the parabola through $(1, 2)$, $(2, 7)$ and $(-1, 4)$.

1. Substitute each point into $y = ax^2 + bx + c$:
$$\begin{cases} a + b + c = 2 & (1) \\ 4a + 2b + c = 7 & (2) \\ a - b + c = 4 & (3) \end{cases}$$
2. (1) $-$ (3): $2b = -2$, so $b = -1$.
3. (2) $-$ (1): $3a + b = 5$, so $3a = 6$ and $a = 2$.
4. From (1): $2 - 1 + c = 2$, so $c = 1$.
5. The parabola is $y = 2x^2 - x + 1$. Check $(2, 7)$: $8 - 2 + 1 = 7$.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 3], "y": [-1, 12], "functions": [{"f": "2*x^2 - x + 1", "label": "y = 2x² - x + 1", "from": -2.4, "to": 2.6}], "points": [{"at": [1, 2], "label": "(1, 2)"}, {"at": [2, 7], "label": "(2, 7)"}, {"at": [-1, 4], "label": "(-1, 4)"}], "caption": "Exactly one parabola passes through the three points"}
```

## An application

### Example 4

A café sold 120 drinks: coffees at $3, teas at $2 and smoothies at $5, taking in $380. It sold twice as many coffees as smoothies. How many of each?

1. Let $c$, $t$, $s$ be the numbers sold. Count: $c + t + s = 120$. Money: $3c + 2t + 5s = 380$. Ratio: $c = 2s$.
2. Substitute $c = 2s$ into the others: $t + 3s = 120$ and $2t + 11s = 380$.
3. From the first, $t = 120 - 3s$. Then $2(120 - 3s) + 11s = 380$, so $240 + 5s = 380$ and $s = 28$.
4. So $c = 56$ and $t = 120 - 84 = 36$. Check: $168 + 72 + 140 = 380$.

When one equation already gives one variable in terms of another, substitution can shortcut the elimination.

## Common mistakes

- Eliminating different variables from the two pairs, leaving (A) and (B) in different unknowns.
- Using the same pair of equations twice, which never brings in the third equation.
- Forgetting to multiply every term, including the constant, when scaling an equation.
- Stopping after two variables; the answer is an ordered triple.
- Checking in only one equation.

## Key points

- Three unknowns need three equations; a solution is an ordered triple $(x, y, z)$.
- Eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations, then solve the resulting $2 \times 2$ system.
- A contradiction means no solution; an equation that reduces to $0 = 0$ signals dependence.
- Three points determine a parabola $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ through a $3 \times 3$ system in $a$, $b$, $c$.

lessons.title: Solving systems with matrices
lessons.body:
In the last lesson you solved three-variable systems by elimination, writing $x$, $y$ and $z$ over and over even though only the numbers were changing. A matrix keeps just the numbers. The moves of elimination become row operations on the matrix, and the bookkeeping becomes a routine that a calculator or computer can carry out for any number of variables. This lesson covers that routine, row reduction, and then briefly a second method that uses an inverse matrix.

## Matrices

A **[[matrix]]** is a rectangular array of numbers in rows and columns, written in brackets. Its **[[dimensions]]** are (number of rows) $\times$ (number of columns), always rows first:

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 5 & 3 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{is a } 2 \times 3 \text{ matrix.}$$

Each number is an **[[entry]]**. The entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is written $a_{ij}$; here $a_{12} = -1$ and $a_{23} = 7$.

## The augmented matrix of a system

To turn a linear system into a matrix, line up the variables in the same order in every equation and copy the coefficients, then the constants after a vertical bar. The result is the system's **[[augmented matrix]]**:

$$\begin{cases} x + 2y - z = 4 \\ 3x - y = 5 \\ y + 4z = -2 \end{cases} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 3 & -1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & -2 \end{array}\right]$$

Each row is one equation and each column left of the bar belongs to one variable. A missing variable gets a 0, as for $z$ in the second equation and $x$ in the third. The part left of the bar is the **[[coefficient matrix]]**.

## Row operations

Three moves change a system into an equivalent one (same solutions). On the matrix they are the **[[row operations]]**:

1. Swap two rows: $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$. (List the equations in a different order.)
2. Multiply a row by a nonzero number: $\tfrac13 R_2 \to R_2$. (Scale an equation.)
3. Add a multiple of one row to another row: $R_2 - 3R_1 \to R_2$. (The elimination step.)

Each move can be undone (swap back, divide by the same number, subtract the same multiple), so no solutions are gained or lost. That's why multiplying by 0 is not allowed: it can't be undone, and it would erase an equation.

## Row echelon form and back-substitution

The goal is a staircase shape called **[[row echelon form]]**:

- the first nonzero entry in each row is a 1 (a leading 1);
- each leading 1 is to the right of the leading 1 in the row above, so everything below a leading 1 is 0;
- any rows of all zeros are at the bottom.

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & * & * & * \\ 0 & 1 & * & * \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & * \end{array}\right]$$

The bottom row then gives the value of $z$, and you back-substitute upward. Working column by column, left to right: get a 1 at the top of the column, then use operation 3 to make every entry below it 0. This process is called **[[Gaussian elimination]]**.

### Example 1

Solve $x + 2y = 5$, $3x - y = 1$.

1. Write the augmented matrix and clear the 3 below the leading 1:
$$\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -1 & 1 \end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{R_2 - 3R_1 \to R_2} \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & -7 & -14 \end{array}\right]$$
The new row 2 is $(3 - 3, -1 - 6, 1 - 15)$. The constant gets the same operation as every other entry.
2. Make the second leading entry 1:
$$\xrightarrow{-\frac17 R_2 \to R_2} \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{array}\right]$$
3. Row 2 says $y = 2$. Row 1 says $x + 2y = 5$, so $x = 1$.
4. Check in the original second equation: $3(1) - 2 = 1$. The solution is $(1, 2)$.

### Example 2

Solve the system from Example 1 of the last lesson:
$$\begin{cases} x + y + z = 6 \\ 2x - y + z = 3 \\ x + 2y - z = 2 \end{cases}$$

1. Clear column 1 below the leading 1:
$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 & 2 \end{array}\right] \xrightarrow[R_3 - R_1 \to R_3]{R_2 - 2R_1 \to R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 & -9 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -4 \end{array}\right]$$
2. Row 3 already has a 1 in column 2, so swap rows 2 and 3 to avoid fractions, then clear below it:
$$\xrightarrow{R_2 \leftrightarrow R_3} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 & -9 \end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{R_3 + 3R_2 \to R_3} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -7 & -21 \end{array}\right]$$
3. $-\tfrac17 R_3 \to R_3$ turns the last row into $[\,0 \;\; 0 \;\; 1 \mid 3\,]$, so $z = 3$.
4. Back-substitute. Row 2: $y - 2(3) = -4$, so $y = 2$. Row 1: $x + 2 + 3 = 6$, so $x = 1$.

The solution is $(1, 2, 3)$, the same as by elimination. You can also keep going instead of back-substituting: use each leading 1 to clear the entries *above* it as well. The result is **[[reduced row echelon form]]** (**[[RREF]]**), where the solution can be read straight off:
$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3 \end{array}\right]$$
Graphing calculators have an `rref` command that does all of this in one step.

## No solution or infinitely many

Row reduction reveals the special cases from the last lesson.

- A row $[\,0 \;\; 0 \;\; 0 \mid c\,]$ with $c \ne 0$ says $0 = c$, which is false: the system is **[[inconsistent]]** (no solution).
- A row of all zeros, $[\,0 \;\; 0 \;\; 0 \mid 0\,]$, says $0 = 0$. If the system is consistent and there are fewer leading 1s than variables, it has infinitely many solutions.

### Example 3

The system $2x + 3y - z = 1$, $x - 2y + 3z = 13$, $3x + y + 2z = 16$ from the last lesson:
$$\xrightarrow{R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -2 & 3 & 13 \\ 2 & 3 & -1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 & 16 \end{array}\right] \xrightarrow[R_3 - 3R_1 \to R_3]{R_2 - 2R_1 \to R_2} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -2 & 3 & 13 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & -25 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & -23 \end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{R_3 - R_2 \to R_3} \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -2 & 3 & 13 \\ 0 & 7 & -7 & -25 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \end{array}\right]$$
The last row reads $0 = 2$, so there is no solution.

## The inverse-matrix method (brief)

A system can also be written as one matrix equation. To multiply a matrix by a column, multiply each row of the matrix entry by entry with the column and add:
$$\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2x + y \\ 5x + 3y \end{bmatrix}.$$
So the system $2x + y = 7$, $5x + 3y = 18$ is $AX = B$, with coefficient matrix $A$, unknowns $X$ and constants $B$.

The **[[identity matrix]]** $I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ acts like the number 1: $IX = X$. The **[[inverse matrix]]** $A^{-1}$ is the matrix with $A^{-1}A = I$, the matrix version of a reciprocal. Multiplying both sides of $AX = B$ on the left by $A^{-1}$ gives
$$X = A^{-1}B.$$
For a $2 \times 2$ matrix there is a formula. If $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$, its **[[determinant]]** is $\det A = ad - bc$, and when $\det A \ne 0$,
$$A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}:$$
swap the diagonal entries, change the signs of the other two, and divide by the determinant. If $\det A = 0$ there is no inverse, and the system does not have exactly one solution.

### Example 4

Solve $2x + y = 7$, $5x + 3y = 18$ with an inverse matrix.

1. $\det A = 2(3) - 1(5) = 1$, so $A^{-1} = \dfrac11\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.
2. $X = A^{-1}B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 18 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 21 - 18 \\ -35 + 36 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
3. So $x = 3$, $y = 1$. Check: $6 + 1 = 7$ and $15 + 3 = 18$.

For $3 \times 3$ systems the inverse is found by calculator (enter $A$ and $B$, then compute $A^{-1}B$). The order matters: matrix multiplication is not commutative, and $BA^{-1}$ isn't even defined here.

## Common mistakes

- Doing a row operation on the coefficients but not on the constant after the bar.
- Forgetting the 0 for a missing variable, which shifts entries into the wrong columns.
- Multiplying a row by 0, or subtracting a row from itself, which destroys an equation.
- Reading $[\,0 \;\; 0 \mid 5\,]$ as "$y = 5$". It says $0 = 5$: no solution.
- In the $2 \times 2$ inverse, dividing by $ad + bc$, or forgetting to swap $a$ and $d$ or to negate $b$ and $c$.

## Key points

- An augmented matrix holds a system's coefficients and constants; each row is an equation, each column a variable.
- Row operations (swap, scale by a nonzero number, add a multiple of another row) produce equivalent systems.
- Reduce to row echelon form and back-substitute, or go on to RREF and read off the solution.
- A row $[\,0 \;\cdots\; 0 \mid c\,]$ with $c \ne 0$ means no solution; a zero row with fewer leading 1s than variables means infinitely many.
- In matrix form $AX = B$, so $X = A^{-1}B$ when $\det A \ne 0$; for $2 \times 2$, $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$.

lessons.title: Polynomial functions: end behavior, zeros, and multiplicity
lessons.body:
Lines and parabolas are the graphs of polynomial functions of degree 1 and 2. This module studies polynomial functions of any degree. Their graphs are smooth, unbroken curves, and a handful of features tell you their shape: how the ends behave, where the graph crosses or touches the $x$-axis, and how many turns it makes. This lesson shows how to read all of that from the equation, especially from its factored form.

## Polynomial functions

A **[[polynomial function]]** has the form

$$f(x) = a_nx^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + a_1x + a_0,$$

with whole-number exponents and $a_n \ne 0$. Its degree is $n$ and $a_n$ is its leading coefficient (as in Algebra 1). The graph of every polynomial function is **[[continuous]]** (no breaks or holes) and **[[smooth]]** (no sharp corners).

## End behavior

**[[End behavior]]** describes what $f(x)$ does as $x$ goes far to the right ($x \to \infty$) or far to the left ($x \to -\infty$). For large $|x|$, the leading term $a_nx^n$ dominates all the others. (For $f(x) = x^3 - 100x$, at $x = 1000$ the $x^3$ term is a billion while $100x$ is only a hundred thousand.) So a polynomial's ends behave like its leading term's ends, which depend only on whether the degree is even or odd and on the sign of the leading coefficient.

| | Leading coefficient $> 0$ | Leading coefficient $< 0$ |
|---|---|---|
| Even degree | up on both ends (like $x^2$) | down on both ends (like $-x^2$) |
| Odd degree | down on the left, up on the right (like $x^3$) | up on the left, down on the right (like $-x^3$) |

In arrow notation, "up on the right" is written: as $x \to \infty$, $f(x) \to \infty$.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 3], "y": [-8, 8], "functions": [{"f": "x^4 - 3*x^2", "label": "x⁴ - 3x²", "from": -2.3, "to": 2.3}, {"f": "x^3 - 3*x", "label": "x³ - 3x", "dashed": true, "from": -2.6, "to": 2.3}], "caption": "Even degree, positive lead: both ends up. Odd degree, positive lead: left down, right up"}
```

### Example 1

Describe the end behavior of $f(x) = -2x^5 + 7x^2 - 1$ and $g(x) = 3x^4 - x^3 + 8$.

1. $f$: degree 5 (odd), leading coefficient $-2$ (negative). As $x \to -\infty$, $f(x) \to \infty$; as $x \to \infty$, $f(x) \to -\infty$. Up on the left, down on the right.
2. $g$: degree 4 (even), leading coefficient 3 (positive). Both ends go up.

## Zeros and factors

A **[[zero]]** of $f$ is a number $c$ with $f(c) = 0$. For real $c$, it's an $x$-intercept of the graph. Zeros and factors are linked: $c$ is a zero exactly when $(x - c)$ is a factor (this is the Factor Theorem of the next lesson). So when a polynomial is factored, its zeros can be read off directly.

## Multiplicity

If $(x - c)$ appears exactly $k$ times as a factor, $c$ is a zero of **[[multiplicity]]** $k$. Multiplicity controls how the graph behaves at the intercept:

- odd multiplicity (1, 3, …): the graph crosses the $x$-axis. With multiplicity 1 it crosses roughly like a line; with 3 it flattens out as it crosses, like $x^3$.
- even multiplicity (2, 4, …): the graph touches the axis and turns back, like $x^2$ at the origin.

Why? Near $x = c$, the other factors are close to some fixed nonzero number, so $f(x)$ behaves like a constant times $(x - c)^k$. When $k$ is even, $(x - c)^k$ doesn't change sign; when $k$ is odd, it does.

### Example 2

Describe the zeros of $f(x) = (x + 2)(x - 1)^2(x - 3)$ and sketch the graph.

1. Zeros: $-2$ (multiplicity 1, crosses), $1$ (multiplicity 2, touches), $3$ (multiplicity 1, crosses).
2. Degree $1 + 2 + 1 = 4$; leading coefficient $1 > 0$: both ends up.
3. $y$-intercept: $f(0) = (2)(1)(-3) = -6$.
4. Sketch from the left: coming down from above, cross at $-2$, go below the axis through $(0, -6)$, come up to touch the axis at 1, go back down, then cross at 3 and rise.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 4], "y": [-10, 8], "functions": [{"f": "(x + 2)*(x - 1)^2*(x - 3)", "label": "f(x) = (x + 2)(x - 1)²(x - 3)", "from": -2.6, "to": 3.6}], "points": [{"at": [-2, 0], "label": "-2"}, {"at": [1, 0], "label": "1 (touch)"}, {"at": [3, 0], "label": "3"}, {"at": [0, -6], "label": "(0, -6)"}], "caption": "Crossing at the odd-multiplicity zeros, touching at the double zero"}
```

The signs between zeros can be checked with test values: $f(2) = (4)(1)(-1) = -4 < 0$, consistent with the graph dipping below the axis between 1 and 3.

## Turning points

A **[[turning point]]** is where the graph changes from rising to falling or vice versa (a local maximum or minimum). A polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n - 1$ turning points, and at most $n$ real zeros. The quartic above has 3 turning points, the maximum possible for degree 4.

These limits work in reverse too: a graph with 4 turning points must have degree at least 5.

## Writing a polynomial from its zeros

### Example 3

Write a cubic polynomial with zeros $-1$, $2$ and $4$ whose graph passes through $(0, 16)$.

1. Factors: $f(x) = a(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 4)$.
2. Use the point: $f(0) = a(1)(-2)(-4) = 8a = 16$, so $a = 2$.
3. $f(x) = 2(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 4)$, or expanded, $2x^3 - 10x^2 + 4x + 16$.

### Example 4

What is the smallest possible degree of a polynomial whose graph touches the axis at $-3$, crosses at 0, and crosses at 5 with a flattened "S" shape?

Touch at $-3$: even multiplicity, at least 2. Cross at 0: at least 1. Flattened crossing at 5: odd multiplicity at least 3. Minimum degree $2 + 1 + 3 = 6$.

## The Intermediate Value Theorem

Because polynomial graphs are continuous, if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs, the graph must cross the $x$-axis somewhere between $a$ and $b$. This is the **[[Intermediate Value Theorem]]** for polynomials. For example, $f(x) = x^3 - x - 1$ has $f(1) = -1$ and $f(2) = 5$, so it has a zero between 1 and 2 (about 1.32), even though that zero isn't a nice number.

## Common mistakes

- Judging end behavior from the first written term instead of the highest-degree term.
- Reading the zero of $(x + 2)$ as 2 instead of $-2$.
- Drawing a crossing at an even-multiplicity zero.
- Forgetting to add multiplicities to get the degree.
- Assuming a degree-$n$ polynomial always has $n$ real zeros; it has at most $n$.

## Key points

- End behavior follows the leading term: even degree, ends match; odd degree, ends go opposite ways; a negative leading coefficient flips the picture.
- $c$ is a zero exactly when $(x - c)$ is a factor.
- Odd multiplicity: the graph crosses. Even multiplicity: it touches and turns back.
- Degree $n$: at most $n$ real zeros and at most $n - 1$ turning points.
- Opposite signs of $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ guarantee a zero between $a$ and $b$.

lessons.title: Polynomial division; the remainder and factor theorems
lessons.body:
To find all the zeros of a polynomial of degree 3 or more, you usually find one zero and then divide out its factor to get a smaller polynomial. This lesson shows how to divide polynomials, by long division and by the faster shortcut called synthetic division, and proves two theorems that tie division to evaluation and to factoring.

## Long division of polynomials

Polynomial long division works exactly like long division of numbers: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, repeat. Write both polynomials in standard form, and include missing powers with coefficient 0.

### Example 1

Divide $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 5$ by $x - 2$.

1. Divide leading terms: $2x^3 \div x = 2x^2$. Multiply: $2x^2(x - 2) = 2x^3 - 4x^2$. Subtract: $(2x^3 - 3x^2) - (2x^3 - 4x^2) = x^2$. Bring down $+4x$: $x^2 + 4x$.
2. $x^2 \div x = x$. Multiply: $x^2 - 2x$. Subtract: $6x$. Bring down $-5$: $6x - 5$.
3. $6x \div x = 6$. Multiply: $6x - 12$. Subtract: $7$.
4. The **[[quotient]]** is $2x^2 + x + 6$ and the **[[remainder]]** is 7.

$$\frac{2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 5}{x - 2} = 2x^2 + x + 6 + \frac{7}{x - 2}.$$

The **[[division algorithm]]** says that for a polynomial $f$ and a nonzero divisor $d$,

$$f(x) = d(x)\,q(x) + r(x),$$

where the remainder $r$ is either 0 or has smaller degree than $d$. Check Example 1: $(x - 2)(2x^2 + x + 6) + 7 = 2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 12 + 7$, which is the original.

### Example 2

Divide $x^4 - 3x^2 + 2x + 1$ by $x^2 + x - 1$.

1. Fill in the missing term: $x^4 + 0x^3 - 3x^2 + 2x + 1$.
2. $x^4 \div x^2 = x^2$. Subtract $x^2(x^2 + x - 1) = x^4 + x^3 - x^2$: left with $-x^3 - 2x^2 + 2x$.
3. $-x^3 \div x^2 = -x$. Subtract $-x(x^2 + x - 1) = -x^3 - x^2 + x$: left with $-x^2 + x + 1$.
4. $-x^2 \div x^2 = -1$. Subtract $-1(x^2 + x - 1) = -x^2 - x + 1$: left with $2x$.
5. Quotient $x^2 - x - 1$, remainder $2x$ (degree 1, less than the divisor's degree 2, so we stop).

## Synthetic division

When the divisor is $x - c$, the work can be compressed into rows of coefficients. This is **[[synthetic division]]**.

1. Write $c$ on the left and the dividend's coefficients (with zeros for missing terms) in a row.
2. Bring down the first coefficient.
3. Multiply it by $c$, write the product under the next coefficient, and add.
4. Repeat to the end. The last number is the remainder; the others are the quotient's coefficients, one degree lower than the dividend.

### Example 3

Divide $2x^3 - 3x^2 + 4x - 5$ by $x - 2$ synthetically.

$$\begin{array}{r|rrrr} 2 & 2 & -3 & 4 & -5 \\ & & 4 & 2 & 12 \\ \hline & 2 & 1 & 6 & 7 \end{array}$$

Bring down 2. $2 \cdot 2 = 4$; $-3 + 4 = 1$. $1 \cdot 2 = 2$; $4 + 2 = 6$. $6 \cdot 2 = 12$; $-5 + 12 = 7$. Quotient $2x^2 + x + 6$, remainder 7, matching Example 1.

For a divisor like $x + 3$, use $c = -3$, since $x + 3 = x - (-3)$.

### Example 4

Divide $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4$ by $x + 1$.

Coefficients $1, 0, -5, 0, 4$ with $c = -1$:

$$\begin{array}{r|rrrrr} -1 & 1 & 0 & -5 & 0 & 4 \\ & & -1 & 1 & 4 & -4 \\ \hline & 1 & -1 & -4 & 4 & 0 \end{array}$$

Quotient $x^3 - x^2 - 4x + 4$, remainder 0. So $x + 1$ is a factor.

## The Remainder Theorem

Put $d(x) = x - c$ in the division algorithm: $f(x) = (x - c)q(x) + r$, where $r$ is a number. Substitute $x = c$: the first term vanishes, leaving $f(c) = r$.

> **[[Remainder Theorem]]**: the remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $x - c$ is $f(c)$.

In Example 1, $f(2) = 16 - 12 + 8 - 5 = 7$, the same as the remainder. This gives a fast way to evaluate polynomials (synthetic division with $c$) and, more importantly, links division to zeros.

## The Factor Theorem

A remainder of 0 means $x - c$ divides $f$ evenly. Combining with the Remainder Theorem:
