cards.front: When does $a(x - h)^2 + k = 0$ have non-real solutions?
cards.back: When $a$ and $k$ have the same sign: the parabola opens away from the $x$-axis.
Factor and cancel. A cancelled factor gives a hole; a denominator factor that remains gives a vertical asymptote.

cards.front: Horizontal asymptote of a rational function
cards.back: Top degree smaller: $y = 0$. Equal: ratio of leading coefficients. Top larger: none.
Vertical $x = h$, horizontal $y = k$.
$y = \dfrac kx$ with $k = xy$ constant; doubling $x$ halves $y$.

cards.front: Solving a line-and-curve system by substitution
cards.back: Solve the linear equation for one variable, substitute into the other, solve the quadratic, then get each partner from the linear equation and check.

cards.front: Number of intersections of a line with a parabola or circle
cards.back: Substitute to get a quadratic: discriminant $> 0$, two points; $= 0$, one (tangent); $< 0$, none.

cards.front: Circle centered at the origin with radius $r$
When to use elimination on a nonlinear system
cards.back: When both equations contain only $x^2$ and $y^2$ terms: add or subtract to eliminate one, then take $\pm$ square roots (up to four solutions).
One row per equation, one column per variable (0 for a missing variable), constants after the bar.
Swap two rows; multiply a row by a nonzero number; add a multiple of one row to another row.
REF: staircase of leading 1s with zeros below them, then back-substitute. RREF: zeros above and below each leading 1, so the solution can be read off.
It says $0 = c$: the system has no solution (inconsistent).
$\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$, when $ad - bc \ne 0$.
$X = A^{-1}B$ (multiply on the left); possible only when $\det A \ne 0$.

cards.front: Steps for a polynomial or rational inequality
cards.back: Get 0 on one side, factor (one fraction), find critical values, test each interval, keep the intervals with the right sign.

cards.front: Critical values of a rational inequality
cards.back: Zeros of the numerator (included for $\le$, $\ge$) and zeros of the denominator (never included).

cards.front: Sign change at a repeated zero
cards.back: The sign changes at a zero of odd multiplicity and stays the same at a zero of even multiplicity.

cards.front: Why not multiply both sides by $x - 3$?
cards.back: Its sign is unknown, so you cannot tell whether to flip the inequality. Subtract to get 0 on one side and use a sign chart.

glossary.definition: A branching diagram that lists the outcomes of a multi-step process; each path from start to end is one outcome. For probability, multiply along a path.
If one choice can be made in $m$ ways and a following choice in $n$ ways, the two can be made together in $m \cdot n$ ways. Extends to any number of steps.
$n! = n(n - 1)(n - 2)\cdots 2 \cdot 1$, the number of ways to order $n$ different objects. By definition $0! = 1$.
An arrangement in which order matters. The number of permutations of $r$ objects from $n$ is $_nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!}$.
A selection in which order does not matter. The number of combinations of $r$ objects from $n$ is $_nC_r = \dbinom{n}{r} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$.
The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment, such as $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ for one roll of a die.
One possible result of an experiment.
A set of outcomes of an experiment, such as "roll an even number."
For equally likely outcomes, $P(A) = \dfrac{\text{number of outcomes in } A}{\text{number of outcomes in the sample space}}$.
The fraction of trials in which an event actually happened: $\dfrac{\text{times it occurred}}{\text{number of trials}}$.
The complement $A^c$ of an event $A$ is every outcome not in $A$; $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$.
Events that cannot happen at the same time, so $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0$ and $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$.
$P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)$. The overlap is subtracted because it was counted twice.
A table of counts for data classified two ways, with one variable in the rows and the other in the columns.
The probability of $B$ given that $A$ has happened: $P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(A)}$.
$P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)$; for independent events this is $P(A) \cdot P(B)$.
Events where knowing one happened does not change the probability of the other: $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$, equivalently $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)P(B)$.
Events that are not independent: the outcome of one changes the probability of the other, as with draws without replacement.
The sum of the values divided by how many there are. The population mean is written $\mu$.
A measure of spread, roughly the typical distance of values from the mean. For a population, $\sigma = \sqrt{\sum (x - \mu)^2 / n}$; the sample version $s$ divides by $n - 1$.
A continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped distribution described by its mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.
The bell-shaped graph of a normal distribution. The total area under it is 1, and the area between two values is the probability of landing between them.
In a normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2 and 99.7% within 3.
The number of standard deviations a value lies from the mean: $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$. Positive above the mean, negative below.
The normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1; z-scores follow it.
A function (on many calculators, normalcdf(lower, upper, μ, σ)) that gives the area under a normal curve between two values, that is, the probability of landing between them.
Lopsided, with a long tail on one side. Skewed data are not normal, so the 68–95–99.7 rule does not apply.
The entire group that a study wants to learn about.
The part of a population that is actually observed or surveyed.
A number that describes a population, such as the true percent of all voters who support a law. Usually unknown.
A number computed from a sample, used to estimate a parameter.
A sample chosen so that every group of $n$ individuals in the population is equally likely to be selected.
A systematic tendency of a sampling method to over- or under-represent part of the population. A larger sample does not remove it.
How far a sample result is likely to be from the population value. For a random sample of size $n$, about $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt n}$ at 95% confidence.
An angle with its vertex at the origin and its initial side along the positive $x$-axis.
The ray where the rotation forming an angle starts; in standard position, the positive $x$-axis.
The ray where the rotation forming an angle ends.
An angle in standard position whose terminal side lies on an axis, such as $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ or $270^\circ$.
The central angle that cuts off an arc equal in length to the radius. $2\pi$ radians $= 360^\circ$, so $\pi$ radians $= 180^\circ$.
Angles in standard position that share a terminal side; they differ by a multiple of $360^\circ$ ($2\pi$).
The acute angle between the terminal side of an angle and the $x$-axis. Trig values of an angle equal those of its reference angle, up to sign.
The length of a piece of a circle: $s = r\theta$, with $\theta$ in radians.
The circle of radius 1 centered at the origin, $x^2 + y^2 = 1$. The point at angle $\theta$ is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$.
For an angle $\theta$ in standard position, the $x$-coordinate of its point on the unit circle. For an acute angle in a right triangle, adjacent over hypotenuse.
For an angle $\theta$ in standard position, the $y$-coordinate of its point on the unit circle. For an acute angle in a right triangle, opposite over hypotenuse.
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$, the ratio $\tfrac{y}{x}$ of the unit-circle point; undefined when $\cos\theta = 0$.
$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ for every angle $\theta$, because the point $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ lies on $x^2 + y^2 = 1$.
A function whose values repeat at regular intervals: $f(x + P) = f(x)$ for all $x$.
The length of the shortest interval over which a periodic function repeats. For $y = a\sin(bx)$ or $a\cos(bx)$ it is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$.
One complete copy of the repeating pattern of a periodic graph.
A graph with the shape of a sine wave: $y = a\sin\big(b(x - h)\big) + k$ or the cosine version.
For a sinusoid, $|a|$: the distance from the midline to a maximum, half the distance from maximum to minimum.
The number of cycles per unit of the input, $\dfrac{b}{2\pi}$; the reciprocal of the period.
The horizontal line $y = k$ halfway between the maximum and minimum of a sinusoid: $k = \dfrac{\max + \min}{2}$.
The horizontal shift $h$ of a sinusoid $y = a\sin\big(b(x - h)\big) + k$; right when $h > 0$. Factor $b$ out first: $\sin(bx - c)$ shifts by $\tfrac{c}{b}$.
A polynomial with two terms, such as $a + b$ or $2x - 3$.
A power of a binomial, such as $(a + b)^n$, written out as a sum of terms.

A triangle of numbers with 1s along the edges in which each other entry is the sum of the two above it. Row $n$ (starting from row 0) lists the coefficients of $(a + b)^n$, which are $_nC_0, {}_nC_1, \ldots, {}_nC_n$.
The numbers $_nC_k = \binom{n}{k} = \dfrac{n!}{k!\,(n - k)!}$, the coefficients in the expansion of $(a + b)^n$.
$(a + b)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} {}_nC_k\, a^{n-k}b^k$ for any whole number $n$; the term containing $b^k$ is the $(k + 1)$st term.
An equation $ax + by + cz = d$; its graph is a plane.
A solution $(x, y, z)$ of an equation or system in three variables.
A number whose square is a given number; every positive number has two square roots.
The nonnegative square root, written $\sqrt{a}$.
$\sqrt[n]{a}$, a number whose $n$th power is $a$ (the nonnegative one when $n$ is even).
In $\sqrt[n]{a}$, the number $n$ that tells which root.
The expression under a radical sign.
An expression $\sqrt[n]{a}$ involving a root.
A radical with no perfect-power factors in the radicand, no fractions under the radical, and no radical in a denominator.
Radicals with the same index and radicand, such as $3\sqrt5$ and $4\sqrt5$; they combine like like terms.
Rewriting a fraction so that no radical appears in its denominator.
For $a + \sqrt b$, the expression $a - \sqrt b$; their product $a^2 - b$ has no radical.
$a^{m/n} = \left(\sqrt[n]{a}\right)^m$: the denominator is the root and the numerator is the power.
An equation with the variable inside a radical.
A value that solves a transformed equation (after squaring or clearing denominators) but not the original equation.
The number $i$ with $i^2 = -1$.
A number $a + bi$ with $a$ and $b$ real.
In $a + bi$, the number $a$.
In $a + bi$, the real number $b$ (not $bi$).
A complex number $bi$ with $b \ne 0$, such as $3i$.
A plane in which $a + bi$ is plotted at $(a, b)$: real parts horizontally, imaginary parts vertically.
The conjugate of $a + bi$ is $a - bi$; their product is $a^2 + b^2$.
A quotient of two polynomials, $\tfrac{P}{Q}$ with $Q$ not the zero polynomial.
Values of the variable that make a denominator zero; they are not in the domain.
$\dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{A}{B}$ for $C \ne 0$: a common factor can be cancelled.
A fraction or rational expression with no common factors left in the numerator and denominator.
A single missing point on a graph, where a factor cancels from the numerator and denominator.
A function given by a rational expression, such as $f(x) = \tfrac1x$.
A vertical line $x = a$ that a graph approaches but never touches, where the function values blow up.
The simplest expression that every denominator divides: each distinct factor to its highest power.
A fraction with a fraction in its numerator, denominator, or both.
An equation containing rational expressions.
An equation of two ratios, $\tfrac ab = \tfrac cd$.
In $\tfrac ab = \tfrac cd$, the products $ad$ and $bc$, which must be equal.
A function $f(x) = a_nx^n + \cdots + a_1x + a_0$ with whole-number exponents.
Having a graph with no breaks, holes or jumps.
Having a graph with no sharp corners.
What $f(x)$ does as $x \to \infty$ and $x \to -\infty$; for a polynomial it follows the leading term.
The number of times a factor $(x - c)$ appears; odd multiplicity crosses the axis, even multiplicity touches it.
A point where a graph changes from rising to falling or the reverse; degree $n$ allows at most $n - 1$.
If a continuous function has $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ of opposite signs, it has a zero between $a$ and $b$.
The result of a division; in $f = d \cdot q + r$, the polynomial $q$.
What is left over in division; in $f = d \cdot q + r$, the polynomial $r$, of smaller degree than $d$.
$f(x) = d(x)q(x) + r(x)$ with $r = 0$ or $\deg r < \deg d$.
A shortcut for dividing a polynomial by $x - c$ using only its coefficients.
The remainder when $f(x)$ is divided by $x - c$ is $f(c)$.
$x - c$ is a factor of $f(x)$ exactly when $f(c) = 0$.
Any rational zero $\tfrac pq$ (lowest terms) of a polynomial with integer coefficients has $p$ dividing the constant term and $q$ dividing the leading coefficient.
The quotient left after dividing out a known factor; its zeros are the remaining zeros.
Every polynomial of degree $n \ge 1$ has a complex zero; hence exactly $n$ complex zeros counting multiplicity.
For polynomials with real coefficients, non-real zeros come as $a \pm bi$.
A function $f(x) = ab^x$ with $b > 0$, $b \ne 1$.
Increase by a constant factor $b > 1$ per unit of time.
Decrease by a constant factor $0 < b < 1$ per unit of time.
A horizontal line that a graph approaches as $x \to \infty$ or $x \to -\infty$; $y = 0$ for $y = b^x$.
The time for a decaying quantity to fall to half its amount: $A = A_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/h}$.
The time for a growing quantity to double: $A = A_0 \cdot 2^{t/d}$.
Interest earned on interest: $A = P\left(1 + \tfrac rn\right)^{nt}$.
The number $e \approx 2.71828$, the limit of $\left(1 + \tfrac1n\right)^n$.
Interest compounded infinitely often: $A = Pe^{rt}$.
The function $f(x) = e^x$.
$\log_b x$ is the exponent $y$ with $b^y = x$ (for $b > 0$, $b \ne 1$, $x > 0$).
The statement $b^y = x$, equivalent to the logarithmic form $\log_b x = y$.
The base-10 logarithm, written $\log x$.
The base-$e$ logarithm, written $\ln x$.
Two functions that undo each other: $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$ and $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$. Their graphs are reflections across $y = x$; for example, $b^x$ and $\log_b x$.
$\log_b x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln b} = \dfrac{\log x}{\log b}$.
An equation with the variable in an exponent, such as $3^x = 20$.
An equation with the variable inside a logarithm, such as $\log_2(x + 1) = 5$.
An ordered list of numbers $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$; a function on the positive integers.
A rule giving $a_n$ directly from $n$, such as $a_n = 3n + 2$.
A rule giving the first term and each term from the previous one, such as $a_1 = 5$, $a_n = a_{n-1} + 3$.
A sequence with a constant difference between terms: $a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d$.
The constant $d = a_n - a_{n-1}$ of an arithmetic sequence.
The sum of the terms of a sequence.
$\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k$ means $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n$.
The sum of an arithmetic sequence: $S_n = \dfrac{n(a_1 + a_n)}{2}$.
A sequence with a constant ratio between terms: $a_n = a_1r^{n-1}$.
The constant $r = \tfrac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}$ of a geometric sequence.
The sum of a geometric sequence: $S_n = \dfrac{a_1(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$ for $r \ne 1$.
$a_1 + a_1r + a_1r^2 + \cdots$; it has the sum $\dfrac{a_1}{1 - r}$ when $|r| < 1$.
Said of an infinite series whose partial sums approach a finite number.
Said of an infinite series that has no finite sum.
Describes a system of equations with no solution; elimination leads to a false statement such as $0 = 2$.
A number $c$ with $f(c) = 0$. Real zeros are the $x$-intercepts of the graph.
In a power $b^x$, the number $b$ being raised to the exponent. In $f(x) = ab^x$ it is the growth or decay factor.
The number $b$ that an exponential function $ab^x$ multiplies by at each step: growth if $b > 1$, decay if $0 < b < 1$.
The simplest function in a family, such as $y = x^2$ or $y = \sqrt x$, from which the others are made by transformations.
A change to a graph's position, orientation or size: a translation, reflection, stretch or compression.
A transformation that slides a graph without turning or resizing it. $y = f(x - h) + k$ moves the graph of $f$ right $h$ and up $k$.
Moving a graph up or down: $y = f(x) + k$ moves the graph of $f$ up $k$ units (down if $k < 0$).
Moving a graph left or right: $y = f(x - h)$ moves the graph of $f$ right $h$ units (left if $h < 0$).
A transformation that flips a graph across a line: $-f(x)$ reflects across the $x$-axis and $f(-x)$ across the $y$-axis.
The graph of $y = af(x)$ with $a > 1$: every point moves away from the $x$-axis, $(x, y) \to (x, ay)$.
The graph of $y = af(x)$ with $0 < a < 1$: every point moves toward the $x$-axis, $(x, y) \to (x, ay)$.
The graph of $y = f(bx)$ with $b > 1$: the graph is squeezed toward the $y$-axis, $(x, y) \to \left(\tfrac xb, y\right)$.
The graph of $y = f(bx)$ with $0 < b < 1$: the graph is pulled away from the $y$-axis, $(x, y) \to \left(\tfrac xb, y\right)$.
A function that uses different formulas on different, non-overlapping intervals of its domain.
In a piecewise function, an input where the rule changes from one formula to another.
A piecewise function that is constant on each piece, so its graph looks like a staircase.
$\lfloor x \rfloor$, the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$; for example $\lfloor 3.7 \rfloor = 3$ and $\lfloor -1.2 \rfloor = -2$.
The function $(f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))$: apply $g$ first, then apply $f$ to the result.
A function formed by composition, such as $f(g(x))$.
To write a function as a composition $f(g(x))$ of simpler functions, as in $(3x + 1)^5$ with $g(x) = 3x + 1$ and $f(x) = x^5$.
A function in which different inputs always give different outputs; exactly the functions that have inverse functions.
A function is one-to-one exactly when no horizontal line crosses its graph more than once.
Keep only part of a function's domain, often so that it becomes one-to-one, as with $y = x^2$ for $x \ge 0$.
Having an inverse function; a function is invertible exactly when it is one-to-one.
A quadratic written as $f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k$; its vertex is $(h, k)$.
Rewriting $x^2 + bx$ as $\left(x + \tfrac b2\right)^2 - \left(\tfrac b2\right)^2$, used to reach vertex form or solve a quadratic.
The solutions of $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$.
The quantity $b^2 - 4ac$. Positive: two real solutions; zero: one double root; negative: two complex conjugate solutions.
A root that occurs twice, as $x = 3$ in $(x - 3)^2 = 0$; the parabola touches the $x$-axis there.
The function $y = \dfrac1x$, with vertical asymptote $x = 0$ and horizontal asymptote $y = 0$.
A slanted line that a graph approaches at its ends; a rational function has one when the numerator's degree is one more than the denominator's.
A relationship $y = \dfrac kx$ ($k \ne 0$): the product $xy$ is constant, so doubling one quantity halves the other.
The constant $k$ in a variation: $k = xy$ for inverse variation and $k = \tfrac yx$ for direct variation.
A relationship $y = kx$ ($k \ne 0$): the ratio $\tfrac yx$ is constant, so the quantities grow together.
A system of equations in which at least one equation is not linear (it has a square, a product of variables, and so on). Its real solutions are the points where the graphs meet.
The set of points at a fixed distance $r$ (the radius) from a center. Centered at the origin its equation is $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$; centered at $(h, k)$ it is $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$.
A rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns, written in brackets.
The size of a matrix, written rows $\times$ columns: a matrix with 2 rows and 3 columns is $2 \times 3$.
One of the numbers in a matrix. The entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is written $a_{ij}$.
A matrix holding a linear system: each row is an equation, the columns left of the bar hold the coefficients of each variable, and the column after the bar holds the constants.
The matrix of a linear system's coefficients only, without the constants; the part of the augmented matrix left of the bar.
The three moves that change an augmented matrix into one for an equivalent system: swap two rows, multiply a row by a nonzero number, or add a multiple of one row to another.

A staircase form of a matrix: the first nonzero entry of each row is a leading 1, each leading 1 is to the right of the one above it (so the entries below it are 0), and any zero rows are at the bottom.
Solving a linear system by using row operations to reach row echelon form, then back-substituting from the bottom row up.
Row echelon form in which each leading 1 is the only nonzero entry in its column, so the solution of the system can be read off directly.
Reduced row echelon form: each leading 1 is the only nonzero entry in its column. Calculators compute it with an rref command.
A square matrix $I$ with 1s on the main diagonal and 0s elsewhere, such as $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$; multiplying by it changes nothing, like multiplying by 1.
For a square matrix $A$, the matrix $A^{-1}$ with $A^{-1}A = AA^{-1} = I$. It exists exactly when $\det A \ne 0$, and then $AX = B$ has the solution $X = A^{-1}B$.
A number computed from a square matrix; for $\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$ it is $ad - bc$. The matrix has an inverse exactly when the determinant is not 0.
In a polynomial or rational inequality, the zeros of the numerator and of the denominator (after moving everything to one side). The sign of the expression can change only at these numbers.
A number line marked with the critical values of an expression and its sign ($+$ or $-$) on each interval between them, used to solve inequalities.
An inequality that can be written as $p(x) > 0$, $p(x) < 0$, $p(x) \ge 0$ or $p(x) \le 0$ for a polynomial $p$.
An inequality with the variable in a denominator, such as $\dfrac{x + 1}{x - 3} \le 0$. Zeros of the denominator are never part of the solution.

references.title: Equations, inequalities, lines, systems and matrices
references.body:
## Properties of real numbers

| Property | Addition | Multiplication |
|---|---|---|
| Commutative | $a + b = b + a$ | $ab = ba$ |
| Associative | $(a + b) + c = a + (b + c)$ | $(ab)c = a(bc)$ |
| Identity | $a + 0 = a$ | $a \cdot 1 = a$ |
| Inverse | $a + (-a) = 0$ | $a \cdot \tfrac1a = 1$ ($a \ne 0$) |
| Distributive | $a(b + c) = ab + ac$ | |

Order of operations: grouping, exponents, multiplication/division (left to right), addition/subtraction (left to right).

## Solving

| Type | Method |
|---|---|
| Linear equation | clear fractions, simplify, collect variable terms, isolate, check |
| Literal equation | treat other letters as numbers; if the variable appears twice, collect and factor |
| Linear inequality | as an equation, but flip the symbol when multiplying or dividing by a negative |
| $\lvert u \rvert = k$ ($k > 0$) | $u = k$ or $u = -k$ |
| $\lvert u \rvert < k$ | $-k < u < k$ |
| $\lvert u \rvert > k$ | $u < -k$ or $u > k$ |

Variable vanishes: false statement means no solution; true statement means all real numbers.

## Interval notation

| Inequality | Interval |
|---|---|
| $a < x < b$ | $(a, b)$ |
| $a \le x \le b$ | $[a, b]$ |
| $x > a$ | $(a, \infty)$ |
| $x \le b$ | $(-\infty, b]$ |

## Lines

| Form | Equation | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Slope | $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ | horizontal: $m = 0$; vertical: undefined |
| Slope-intercept | $y = mx + b$ | $y$-intercept $(0, b)$ |
| Point-slope | $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$ | |
| Standard | $Ax + By = C$ | slope $-\tfrac AB$ |
| Horizontal / vertical | $y = b$ / $x = a$ | |
| Parallel | $m_1 = m_2$ | different intercepts |
| Perpendicular | $m_1m_2 = -1$ | $m_2 = -\tfrac{1}{m_1}$ (neither line vertical) |

## Systems

| Outcome | Graph | Algebra |
|---|---|---|
| one solution | lines cross | values for each variable |
| no solution | parallel lines | false statement, e.g. $0 = 5$ |
| infinitely many | same line | true statement, e.g. $0 = 0$ |

Three variables: eliminate the same variable from two different pairs of equations, solve the $2 \times 2$ system, back-substitute.

## Nonlinear systems

| Method | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Substitution | one equation is linear | solve it for a variable, substitute, solve the quadratic; partners from the linear equation |
| Elimination | only $x^2$ and $y^2$ terms | add or subtract, then take $\pm$ square roots (up to 4 solutions) |
| Discriminant of the substituted quadratic | counting intersections | $> 0$: two; $= 0$: one (tangent); $< 0$: none |

Circle: $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$ (center origin), $(x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2$ (center $(h, k)$).

## Matrices

| Idea | Statement |
|---|---|
| Augmented matrix | rows = equations, columns = variables (0 if missing), constants after the bar |
| Row operations | $R_i \leftrightarrow R_j$; $cR_i \to R_i$ ($c \ne 0$); $R_i + cR_j \to R_i$ |
| Row echelon form | leading 1s in a staircase, zeros below; back-substitute |
| RREF | zeros above and below each leading 1; read off the solution |
| $[\,0 \;\cdots\; 0 \mid c\,]$, $c \ne 0$ | no solution |
| Determinant ($2 \times 2$) | $\det\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} = ad - bc$ |
| Inverse ($2 \times 2$) | $\dfrac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{bmatrix}$, if $ad - bc \ne 0$ |
| Matrix equation | $AX = B \Rightarrow X = A^{-1}B$ |

Linear programming: the maximum or minimum of a linear objective on a polygonal feasible region occurs at a vertex.

## Useful formulas

| Formula | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $d = rt$ | distance = rate × time |
| $I = Prt$ | simple interest |
| $\dfrac{\text{new} - \text{old}}{\text{old}} \times 100\%$ | percent change |
| $P = 2l + 2w$, $A = lw$ | rectangle |

references.title: Exponentials, logarithms and sequences
references.body:
## Exponential models

| Model | Formula |
|---|---|
| Exponential function | $f(x) = ab^x$ (growth $b > 1$, decay $0 < b < 1$) |
| Percent growth / decay | $A = a(1 \pm r)^t$ |
| Half-life $h$ | $A = A_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/h}$ |
| Doubling time $d$ | $A = A_0 \cdot 2^{t/d}$ |
| Compound interest | $A = P\left(1 + \tfrac rn\right)^{nt}$ |
| Continuous compounding | $A = Pe^{rt}$, $e \approx 2.71828$ |

## Logarithms ($b > 0$, $b \ne 1$, $M, N > 0$)

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| Definition | $\log_b x = y \iff b^y = x$ |
| Special values | $\log_b 1 = 0$, $\log_b b = 1$ |
| Inverses | $\log_b b^x = x$, $b^{\log_b x} = x$ |
| Product | $\log_b(MN) = \log_b M + \log_b N$ |
| Quotient | $\log_b \tfrac MN = \log_b M - \log_b N$ |
| Power | $\log_b M^k = k\log_b M$ |
| Change of base | $\log_b x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln b} = \dfrac{\log x}{\log b}$ |

No rule exists for $\log_b(M + N)$. $\log x$ means base 10; $\ln x$ means base $e$.

## Solving equations

| Equation | Method |
|---|---|
| $b^{f(x)} = b^{g(x)}$ | set $f(x) = g(x)$ |
| $b^{f(x)} = c$ | isolate, take $\ln$: $f(x) = \dfrac{\ln c}{\ln b}$ |
| $\log_b f(x) = c$ | $f(x) = b^c$; check arguments are positive |
| $\log_b f(x) = \log_b g(x)$ | $f(x) = g(x)$; check |
| Doubling time | $t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + r)}$ |

## Sequences and series

| | Arithmetic | Geometric |
|---|---|---|
| Rule | add $d$ | multiply by $r$ |
| $n$th term | $a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d$ | $a_n = a_1r^{n-1}$ |
| Sum of $n$ terms | $S_n = \dfrac{n(a_1 + a_n)}{2}$ | $S_n = \dfrac{a_1(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$ |
| Infinite sum | diverges (unless all terms 0) | $S = \dfrac{a_1}{1 - r}$ if $\lvert r \rvert < 1$ |

Sigma notation: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n$.

references.title: Functions, quadratics, radicals, rational functions and polynomials
references.body:
## Functions

| Idea | Rule |
|---|---|
| Function | each input has exactly one output (vertical line test) |
| Domain from a formula | exclude zeros of denominators and negative even-root radicands |
| Composition | $f(g(x))$: apply $g$ first |
| Zeros | solutions of $f(x) = 0$ = $x$-intercepts |
| Average rate of change | $\dfrac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$ |
| Sum, product, quotient | $(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)$, etc.; domain: both defined, and $g(x) \ne 0$ for $\tfrac fg$ |
| Domain of $f(g(x))$ | $x$ in the domain of $g$ and $g(x)$ in the domain of $f$ |
| Inverse | $f(a) = b \iff f^{-1}(b) = a$; exists when $f$ is one-to-one (horizontal line test) |
| Finding $f^{-1}$ | $y = f(x)$, swap $x$ and $y$, solve for $y$; graph reflects across $y = x$ |
| Checking an inverse | $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$ and $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$ |
| Absolute value | $\lvert x \rvert = x$ if $x \ge 0$, $-x$ if $x < 0$ |
| Greatest integer | $\lfloor x \rfloor$ = greatest integer $\le x$; $\lfloor -1.2 \rfloor = -2$ |

## Transformations of $y = f(x)$

| Formula | Effect on the graph | Points move |
|---|---|---|
| $f(x) + k$ | up $k$ (down if $k < 0$) | $(x, y + k)$ |
| $f(x - h)$ | right $h$ (left if $h < 0$) | $(x + h, y)$ |
| $-f(x)$ | reflect across the $x$-axis | $(x, -y)$ |
| $f(-x)$ | reflect across the $y$-axis | $(-x, y)$ |
| $a f(x)$, $a > 0$ | vertical stretch ($a > 1$) or compression ($a < 1$) | $(x, ay)$ |
| $f(bx)$, $b > 0$ | horizontal compression ($b > 1$) or stretch ($b < 1$) | $\left(\tfrac xb, y\right)$ |
| $a f(x - h) + k$ | all together; anchor point to $(h, k)$ | $(x + h, ay + k)$ |

Parent functions: $x$, $x^2$, $x^3$, $\lvert x \rvert$, $\sqrt x$ ($x \ge 0$), $\sqrt[3]x$, $\tfrac1x$ ($x \ne 0$), $2^x$ (asymptote $y = 0$).

## Quadratics

| Fact | Statement |
|---|---|
| Vertex form | $a(x - h)^2 + k$, vertex $(h, k)$ |
| Quadratic formula | $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$ |
| Discriminant | $b^2 - 4ac$: $> 0$ two real, $= 0$ double root, $< 0$ two complex conjugates |
| Sum and product of roots | $r + s = -\tfrac ba$, $rs = \tfrac ca$ |
| Roots $p \pm qi$ | $(x - p)^2 + q^2 = x^2 - 2px + p^2 + q^2$ |

## Radicals and rational exponents

| Rule | Statement |
|---|---|
| Root as exponent | $\sqrt[n]{a} = a^{1/n}$, $a^{m/n} = \left(\sqrt[n]a\right)^m$ |
| Product, quotient | $\sqrt[n]{ab} = \sqrt[n]a\sqrt[n]b$, $\sqrt[n]{\tfrac ab} = \tfrac{\sqrt[n]a}{\sqrt[n]b}$ ($a, b \ge 0$ if $n$ is even; $b \ne 0$) |
| Square of a root | $\sqrt{x^2} = \lvert x \rvert$ |
| Conjugates | $(a + \sqrt b)(a - \sqrt b) = a^2 - b$ |

Radical equations: isolate the radical, raise both sides to the index power, solve, check for extraneous solutions. For $u^{m/n} = c$, raise to the power $\tfrac nm$, with $\pm$ when $m$ is even ($x^{2/3} = 4$ gives $x = \pm 8$).

## Complex numbers

| Fact | Statement |
|---|---|
| Imaginary unit | $i^2 = -1$, $\sqrt{-b} = i\sqrt b$ ($b > 0$) |
| Powers of $i$ | $i, -1, -i, 1$ repeating |
| Conjugate product | $(a + bi)(a - bi) = a^2 + b^2$ |
| Division | multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator |

## Rational expressions

| Task | Method |
|---|---|
| Simplify | factor, note excluded values, cancel common factors only |
| Multiply / divide | factor and cancel; divide = multiply by the reciprocal |
| Add / subtract | rewrite over the LCD (each factor to its highest power) |
| Complex fraction | multiply top and bottom by the LCD of the inner fractions |
| Rational equation | multiply by the LCD, solve, reject excluded values |
| Work | $\dfrac{1}{t_1} + \dfrac{1}{t_2} = \dfrac{1}{T}$ |

## Graphs of rational functions

| Feature | How to find it |
|---|---|
| Domain | exclude zeros of the denominator |
| Hole | a factor that cancels; height from the simplified form |
| Vertical asymptote | a zero of the denominator that remains after cancelling |
| Horizontal asymptote | degree top < bottom: $y = 0$; equal: ratio of leading coefficients; top > bottom: none |
| Intercepts | $x$: zeros of the simplified numerator; $y$: $f(0)$ |
| Transformed reciprocal | $y = \dfrac{a}{x - h} + k$: asymptotes $x = h$, $y = k$ |
| Inverse variation | $y = \dfrac kx$, $k = xy$ |

## Polynomial and rational inequalities

| Step | What to do |
|---|---|
| 1 | Get 0 on one side; combine into one fraction (never multiply by an expression in $x$) |
| 2 | Factor; critical values = zeros of the numerator and of the denominator |
| 3 | Test one value per interval (or multiply factor signs) |
| 4 | Keep intervals with the right sign; include numerator zeros for $\le$, $\ge$; never denominator zeros |

The sign changes at a zero of odd multiplicity and not at a zero of even multiplicity.

## Polynomial functions

| Fact | Statement |
|---|---|
| End behavior | follows $a_nx^n$: even degree, ends match; odd degree, ends opposite |
| Multiplicity | odd: crosses the axis; even: touches and turns |
| Bounds | degree $n$: at most $n$ real zeros, at most $n - 1$ turning points |
| Division algorithm | $f = d \cdot q + r$, $\deg r < \deg d$ |
| Remainder Theorem | remainder of $f(x) \div (x - c)$ is $f(c)$ |
| Factor Theorem | $(x - c)$ is a factor $\iff f(c) = 0$ |
| Rational Root Theorem | candidates $\pm\dfrac{\text{factors of } a_0}{\text{factors of } a_n}$ |
| Fundamental Theorem of Algebra | exactly $n$ complex zeros (with multiplicity); non-real zeros of real polynomials come in conjugate pairs |

references.title: Probability, statistics and trigonometry
references.body:
## Counting

| Idea | Formula | Use when |
|---|---|---|
| Counting principle | $m \cdot n \cdot \ldots$ | A sequence of choices: multiply the options at each step |
| Factorial | $n! = n(n - 1)\cdots 1$, $0! = 1$ | Orders of $n$ different objects |
| Permutations | $_nP_r = \dfrac{n!}{(n - r)!}$ | Choose $r$ of $n$, order matters (ranks, titles, codes without repeats) |
| Combinations | $_nC_r = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$ | Choose $r$ of $n$, order doesn't matter (groups, hands, committees) |
| Repeated objects | $\dfrac{n!}{a!\,b!\cdots}$ | Arrangements when $a$, $b$, … objects are identical |

Repeats allowed (PINs, plates): $n^r$. Symmetry: $_nC_r = {}_nC_{n-r}$.

## Binomial theorem

| Idea | Formula |
|---|---|
| Binomial theorem | $(a + b)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} {}_nC_k\, a^{n-k}b^k$ |
| Term containing $b^k$ | $_nC_k\, a^{n-k}b^k$, the $(k + 1)$st term |
| Pascal's triangle | row $n$ is $_nC_0, \ldots, {}_nC_n$; each entry is the sum of the two above; row sum $2^n$ |

Rows 0 to 6: 1; 1 1; 1 2 1; 1 3 3 1; 1 4 6 4 1; 1 5 10 10 5 1; 1 6 15 20 15 6 1.

## Probability

| Rule | Formula |
|---|---|
| Equally likely outcomes | $P(A) = \dfrac{\text{favorable}}{\text{total}}$ |
| Complement | $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$ |
| "At least one" | $1 - P(\text{none})$ |
| Addition ("or") | $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)$ |
| Mutually exclusive | $P(A \text{ and } B) = 0$, so $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$ |
| Conditional ("given") | $P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(A)}$ |
| Multiplication ("and") | $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$ |
| Independent | $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$, so $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)\,P(B)$ |

Two-way table: for $P(\,\cdot \mid A)$, divide by the total of the row or column for $A$.

## Normal distribution

| Idea | Formula |
|---|---|
| Population standard deviation | $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \mu)^2}{n}}$ (sample $s$ divides by $n - 1$) |
| z-score | $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$ |
| Area between $a$ and $b$ | `normalcdf(a, b, μ, σ)`, or table area left of $z_b$ minus left of $z_a$ |
| Value at a percentile $p$ | `invNorm(p, μ, σ)` |
| Margin of error (95%, quick) | $\approx \dfrac{1}{\sqrt n}$ |

68–95–99.7 rule: about 68% within $1\sigma$, 95% within $2\sigma$, 99.7% within $3\sigma$ of $\mu$.

| Below | $\mu - 3\sigma$ | $\mu - 2\sigma$ | $\mu - \sigma$ | $\mu$ | $\mu + \sigma$ | $\mu + 2\sigma$ | $\mu + 3\sigma$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Percent | 0.15% | 2.5% | 16% | 50% | 84% | 97.5% | 99.85% |

| z | 0.5 | 1 | 1.28 | 1.5 | 1.645 | 1.96 | 2 | 2.5 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Area left of z | 0.6915 | 0.8413 | 0.8997 | 0.9332 | 0.9500 | 0.9750 | 0.9772 | 0.9938 | 0.9987 |

Area left of $-z$ = $1 -$ area left of $z$.

## Angles and the unit circle

| Idea | Formula |
|---|---|
| Degrees ↔ radians | $180^\circ = \pi$; multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ}$ or $\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}$ |
| Arc length | $s = r\theta$ ($\theta$ in radians) |
| Coterminal angles | $\theta + 360^\circ k$ or $\theta + 2\pi k$ |
| Unit circle point | $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$; $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$ |
| Pythagorean identity | $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$ |

| $\theta$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi}{6}$ (30°) | $\frac{\pi}{4}$ (45°) | $\frac{\pi}{3}$ (60°) | $\frac{\pi}{2}$ (90°) | $\pi$ (180°) | $\frac{3\pi}{2}$ (270°) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin\theta$ | $0$ | $\frac12$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $1$ | $0$ | $-1$ |
| $\cos\theta$ | $1$ | $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\frac{\sqrt2}{2}$ | $\frac12$ | $0$ | $-1$ | $0$ |

| Quadrant | Reference angle | $\sin$ | $\cos$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | $\theta$ | + | + |
| II | $180^\circ - \theta$ | + | − |
| III | $\theta - 180^\circ$ | − | − |
| IV | $360^\circ - \theta$ | − | + |

## Sinusoids

$y = a\sin\big(b(x - h)\big) + k$ or $y = a\cos\big(b(x - h)\big) + k$, $b > 0$:

| Feature | Value |
|---|---|
| Amplitude | $\lvert a \rvert = \dfrac{\max - \min}{2}$ |
| Period | $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$ (so $b = \dfrac{2\pi}{\text{period}}$) |
| Frequency | $\dfrac{b}{2\pi}$ cycles per unit |
| Midline | $y = k = \dfrac{\max + \min}{2}$ |
| Phase shift | $h$ (right if $h > 0$); factor $b$ out of $bx - c$ first |

Starting points: $\sin$ starts on the midline going up, $\cos$ at a maximum, $-\cos$ at a minimum. Key points are a quarter period apart.

drills.title: Move a point through a transformation
drills.prompt: The point $({p}, {q})$ is on the graph of $y = f(x)$. Find the matching point on the graph of $y = {a:coef}f(x {nh:signed}) {k:signed}$.
drills.solution:
Write the function as $a\,f(x - h) + k$ with $h = {h}$, $a = {a}$, $k = {k}$. Points move by $(x, y) \to (x + h,\; ay + k)$: multiply the height first, then add.
New $x$: ${p} + ({h}) = {nx}$. New $y$: ${a}({q}) + ({k}) = {aq} + ({k}) = {ny}$. The point is **$({nx}, {ny})$**.
Check: at $x = {nx}$ the inside is ${nx} {nh:signed} = {p}$, so the output is ${a}f({p}) + ({k}) = {ny}$.

drills.title: Vertex and intercept of a transformed absolute value
drills.prompt: For $g(x) = {a:coef}\lvert x {nh:signed} \rvert {k:signed}$, find the vertex (corner point) and the $y$-intercept $g(0)$.
drills.solution:
In $a\lvert x - h \rvert + k$ the corner of $y = \lvert x \rvert$ moves to $(h, k)$. The inside $x {nh:signed}$ is zero at $x = {h}$, so the vertex is **$({h}, {k})$**.
$y$-intercept: $g(0) = {a}\lvert {nh} \rvert + ({k}) = {a}({ah}) + ({k}) =$ **{yint}**.

drills.title: Write the equation of a transformed graph

choices.label: reflected across the $x$-axis
not reflected
right
left
up
down

drills.prompt: The graph of $y = {parent}$ is stretched vertically by a factor of {s}, {refl}, and then shifted {hdir} {hm} and {kdir} {km}. Write the equation of the new graph.
drills.solution:
Use $y = a(x - h)^{n} + k$. The stretch and reflection give $a = {a}$. Shifting {hdir} {hm} is the inside change $x \to x - ({h})$, and shifting {kdir} {km} is the outside change $k = {k}$.
So $y =$ **${a:coef}(x {nh:signed})^{n} {k:signed}$**. Its anchor point (vertex or center) is $({h}, {k})$.

drills.title: Evaluate a piecewise function
drills.prompt:
Let $f(x) = \begin{cases} {a:coef}x {b:signed} & \text{if } x < {c} \\ x^2 {e:signed} & \text{if } x \ge {c} \end{cases}$

Find $f({t1})$ and $f({t2})$.

drills.title: Write an absolute value as a piecewise function
drills.prompt: Write $g(x) = \lvert {a:coef}x {b:signed} \rvert$ as a piecewise function $g(x) = \begin{cases} P(x) & \text{if } x \ge c \\ Q(x) & \text{if } x < c \end{cases}$. Find the break point $c$ (exact) and the linear formulas $P$ and $Q$.
drills.solution:
The break point is where the inside is zero: ${a:coef}x {b:signed} = 0$ gives $c =$ **${c:texfrac}$**.
For $x \ge {c:texfrac}$ the inside is nonnegative, so $P(x) =$ **${a:coef}x {b:signed}$**. For $x < {c:texfrac}$ it's negative and the absolute value changes its sign: $Q(x) = -({a:coef}x {b:signed}) =$ **${na:coef}x {nb:signed}$**.

drills.title: Cost from a step function
drills.prompt: A parking garage charges \${base} for the first hour or less and \${r} for each additional hour or part of an hour. How much does it cost to park for {t} hours?
drills.solution:
After the first hour there are ${extra}$ more hours. Each started hour counts as a whole one, so round up: {blocks} additional charges.
Cost: ${base} + {r} \cdot {blocks} =$ **{cost:money}**.

drills.title: Product and difference of functions
drills.prompt: Let $f(x) = {a:coef}x {b:signed}$ and $g(x) = {c:coef}x {d:signed}$. Find $(fg)(x)$ and $(f - g)(x)$ in simplified form.
drills.solution:
Product: $({a:coef}x {b:signed})({c:coef}x {d:signed}) = {p2:coef}x^2 + ({a})({d})x + ({b})({c})x + ({b})({d}) =$ **${p2:coef}x^2 {p1:signedcoef}x {p0:signed}$**.
Difference: subtract all of $g$: ${a:coef}x {b:signed} {nc:signedcoef}x {nd:signed} =$ **${m1:coef}x {m0:signed}$**.

drills.title: Evaluate compositions
drills.prompt: Let $f(x) = {a:coef}x {b:signed}$ and $g(x) = x^2 {c:signed}$. Find $(f \circ g)({t})$ and $(g \circ f)({t})$.
drills.solution:
Work from the inside out.
$(f \circ g)({t}) = f(g({t}))$: first $g({t}) = ({t})^2 + ({c}) = {gt}$, then $f({gt}) = {a}({gt}) + ({b}) =$ **{fgt}**.
$(g \circ f)({t}) = g(f({t}))$: first $f({t}) = {a}({t}) + ({b}) = {ft}$, then $g({ft}) = {ft2} + ({c}) =$ **{gft}**.

drills.title: Find composition formulas
drills.prompt: Let $f(x) = x^2 {c:signed}$ and $g(x) = {a:coef}x {b:signed}$. Find $f(g(x))$ and $g(f(x))$, expanded.
drills.solution:
$f(g(x))$: put $g(x)$ into every $x$ of $f$: $({a:coef}x {b:signed})^2 + ({c}) = {A:coef}x^2 {B:signedcoef}x + {bb} + ({c})$, which is **${A:coef}x^2 {B:signedcoef}x {C:signed}$**.
$g(f(x))$: ${a}(x^2 {c:signed}) + ({b}) =$ **${a:coef}x^2 {D:signed}$**. The two orders give different functions.

drills.title: Inverse of a linear function
drills.prompt: Find the inverse of $f(x) = {a:coef}x {b:signed}$, and use it to find $f^{-1}({v})$.
drills.solution:
Write $y = {a:coef}x {b:signed}$ and swap: $x = {a:coef}y {b:signed}$. Then ${a:coef}y = x {nb:signed}$, so $f^{-1}(x) =$ **$\dfrac{x {nb:signed}}{{a}}$**.
$f^{-1}({v}) = \dfrac{{v} {nb:signed}}{{a}} =$ **{s}**. Check: $f({s}) = {a}({s}) + ({b}) = {v}$.

drills.title: Find an inverse value without a formula
drills.prompt: The function $f(x) = x^3 + x {c:signed}$ is always increasing, so it is one-to-one. Find $f^{-1}({v})$. (Hint: $f^{-1}({v})$ is the input that gives the output ${v}$; try small integers.)
drills.solution:
We need the $x$ with $f(x) = {v}$, that is, $x^3 + x {c:signed} = {v}$. Testing integers: $f({s}) = {s3} + ({s}) + ({c}) = {v}$.
So $f^{-1}({v}) =$ **{s}**. Because $f$ is increasing, no other input gives ${v}$.

drills.title: Inverse of a rational function
drills.prompt: Find the inverse of $f(x) = \dfrac{{a:coef}x {b:signed}}{x {nc:signed}}$.
drills.solution:
Swap $x$ and $y$: $x = \dfrac{{a:coef}y {b:signed}}{y {nc:signed}}$. Clear the fraction: $x(y {nc:signed}) = {a:coef}y {b:signed}$, so $xy {nc:signedcoef}x = {a:coef}y {b:signed}$.
Collect the $y$ terms: $xy {na:signedcoef}y = {c:coef}x {b:signed}$, so $y(x {na:signed}) = {c:coef}x {b:signed}$.
$f^{-1}(x) =$ **$\dfrac{{c:coef}x {b:signed}}{x {na:signed}}$**. (Its excluded value, ${a}$, is the horizontal asymptote of $f$, a value $f$ never outputs.)

drills.title: Multiply complex numbers
drills.prompt: Multiply $({a} {b:signedcoef}i)({c} {d:signedcoef}i)$ and write the result as $a + bi$.
drills.solution:
FOIL, then use $i^2 = -1$: the $i^2$ term is ${bd}i^2 = {nbd}$.
Real part $({a})({c}) + ({nbd}) =$ **{re}**; imaginary part ${a}({d}) + ({b})({c}) =$ **{im}**.

drills.title: Divide complex numbers
drills.prompt: Write $\dfrac{{a} {b:signedcoef}i}{{c} {d:signedcoef}i}$ in the form $a + bi$. Give exact fractions.
drills.solution:
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate ${c} {nd:signedcoef}i$. The denominator becomes ${c}^2 + ({d})^2 = {den}$, and the numerator becomes ${nre} {nim:signedcoef}i$.
Divide each part by {den}: the real part is $\dfrac{{nre}}{{den}} =$ **${re:texfrac}$** and the imaginary part is $\dfrac{{nim}}{{den}} =$ **${im:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Powers of i
drills.prompt: Simplify ${a:coef}i^{{n}}$ and give its real and imaginary parts.
drills.solution:
Powers of $i$ repeat every 4. ${n} = 4 \cdot {qq} + {r}$, so $i^{{n}} = i^{{r}}$ (the cycle is $i^0 = 1$, $i^1 = i$, $i^2 = -1$, $i^3 = -i$).
Real part **{re}**, imaginary part **{im}**.

drills.title: Solve a 3×3 system
drills.prompt:
Solve the system:

$$\begin{cases} {a1:coef}x {b1:signedcoef}y {c1:signedcoef}z = {d1} \\ {a2:coef}x {b2:signedcoef}y {c2:signedcoef}z = {d2} \\ {a3:coef}x {b3:signedcoef}y {c3:signedcoef}z = {d3} \end{cases}$$
drills.solution:
Eliminate one variable (say $z$) from two different pairs of equations to get two equations in $x$ and $y$; solve that pair, then back-substitute.
The solution is **$({xs}, {ys}, {zs})$**. Check the first equation: ${a1}({xs}) + ({b1})({ys}) + ({c1})({zs}) = {d1}$.

drills.title: Parabola through three points
drills.prompt: Find $a$, $b$ and $c$ so that $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ passes through $({u}, {fu})$, $({v}, {fv})$ and $({w}, {fw})$.
drills.solution:
Substitute each point to get three linear equations in $a$, $b$, $c$, for example ${fu} = a({u})^2 + b({u}) + c$.
Solving the system gives **$a = {a}$, $b = {b}$, $c = {c}$**, so $y = {a:coef}x^2 + ({b})x + ({c})$.

drills.title: Solve a quadratic in vertex form
drills.prompt: Solve ${a:coef}(x {nh:signed})^2 {k:signed} = 0$. The solutions have the form $p \pm qi$ with $q > 0$. Give $p$ and $q$ exactly (you can type a root as sqrt(5)).
drills.solution:
Isolate the square: ${a:coef}(x {nh:signed})^2 = {nk}$, so $(x {nh:signed})^2 = \dfrac{{nk}}{{a}} = -{m}$.
Take square roots: $x {nh:signed} = \pm\sqrt{-{m}} = \pm i\sqrt{{m}}$, so $x = {h} \pm i\sqrt{{m}}$.
So $p =$ **{h}** and $q = \sqrt{{m}} \approx$ **{q:num2}**. (Since $a = {a}$ and $k = {k}$ have the same sign, the parabola opens away from the $x$-axis from its vertex $({h}, {k})$ and never crosses it, which is why the solutions aren't real.)

drills.title: Quadratic formula with a negative discriminant
drills.prompt: Solve ${a:coef}x^2 {b:signedcoef}x {c:signed} = 0$ with the quadratic formula. The solutions are $p \pm qi$ with $q > 0$; give $p$ and $q$.
drills.solution:
Discriminant: $b^2 - 4ac = ({b})^2 - 4({a})({c}) = {disc}$, which is negative, so the solutions are complex conjugates.
$\sqrt{{disc}} = i\sqrt{{nd}} = {rt}i$. Then $x = \dfrac{{nb} \pm {rt}i}{{twoa}}$; divide both terms by ${twoa}$: $x = {p} \pm {q:coef}i$.
So $p =$ **{p}** and $q =$ **{q}**.

drills.title: Build a quadratic from complex roots
drills.prompt: Find $b$ and $c$ so that $y = {a:coef}x^2 + bx + c$ has roots ${p} \pm {q:coef}i$.
drills.solution:
Roots $p \pm qi$ come from $(x - p)^2 + q^2$: here $(x {np:signed})^2 + {q2} = x^2 {m2p:signedcoef}x + {pq}$.
Multiply by the leading coefficient ${a}$: ${a:coef}x^2 {b:signedcoef}x {c:signed}$. So $b =$ **{b}** and $c =$ **{c}**.
Check: the roots add to $2({p})$, which equals $-\tfrac ba = -\tfrac{{b}}{{a}}$, and multiply to $({p})^2 + {q2} = {pq}$, which equals $\tfrac ca = \tfrac{{c}}{{a}}$.

drills.title: Line and parabola
drills.prompt: Solve the system $y = x^2 {p:signedcoef}x {q:signed}$ and $y = {m:coef}x {k:signed}$. Enter the intersection point with the smaller $x$-coordinate first.
drills.solution:
Set the right sides equal: $x^2 {p:signedcoef}x {q:signed} = {m:coef}x {k:signed}$. Move everything to the left: $x^2 {a:signedcoef}x {c:signed} = 0$, which factors as $(x {nr1:signed})(x {nr2:signed}) = 0$. So $x = {r1}$ or $x = {r2}$.
Find each partner from the line: $y = {m}({r1}) {k:signed} = {y1}$ and $y = {m}({r2}) {k:signed} = {y2}$.
The intersection points are **$({r1}, {y1})$** and **$({r2}, {y2})$**.

drills.title: Line and circle
drills.prompt: Solve the system $x^2 + y^2 = {R}$ and $y = {m:coef}x {k:signed}$. Enter the intersection point with the smaller $x$-coordinate first.
drills.solution:
Substitute the line into the circle: $x^2 + ({m:coef}x {k:signed})^2 = {R}$. Expanding the square and collecting terms gives ${A}x^2 {B:signedcoef}x {C:signed} = 0$.
Solve it (factor, or use the quadratic formula): $x = {xa}$ or $x = {xb}$.
Find each partner from the line: $y = {m}({xa}) {k:signed} = {ya}$ and $y = {m}({xb}) {k:signed} = {yb}$.
The points are **$({xa}, {ya})$** and **$({xb}, {yb})$**. Check one in the circle: $({xa})^2 + ({ya})^2 = {R}$.

drills.title: Elimination with x² and y²

choices.label: Each of $x$ and $y$ has two square roots, and only squares appear in the equations, so every sign combination works: there are **4** solutions in all.
Each of $x$ and $y$ has two square roots, and only squares appear in the equations, so every sign combination works: there are **4** solutions in all.
Here $x$ has two square roots but $y$ can only be 0, so there are just **2** solutions in all.

drills.prompt:
Solve the system

$$\begin{cases} {a:coef}x^2 {b:signedcoef}y^2 = {c1} \\ {d:coef}x^2 {e:signedcoef}y^2 = {c2} \end{cases}$$

Enter the solution with $x > 0$ and $y \ge 0$, then the total number of real solutions.

drills.title: Row-reduce a 2×2 system
drills.prompt: Solve the system $x {b1:signedcoef}y = {c1}$, ${a2}x {b2:signedcoef}y = {c2}$ by writing its augmented matrix and row-reducing.
drills.solution:
The augmented matrix already has a leading 1 in row 1. Clear the entry below it:
$$\left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & {b1} & {c1} \\ {a2} & {b2} & {c2} \end{array}\right] \xrightarrow{R_2 - ({a2})R_1 \to R_2} \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & {b1} & {c1} \\ 0 & {p} & {qq} \end{array}\right]$$
Row 2 says ${p:coef}y = {qq}$, so **$y = {ys}$**. Row 1 says $x + ({b1})({ys}) = {c1}$, so $x = {c1} - ({by})$, which gives **$x = {xs}$**.

drills.title: Perform a row operation
drills.prompt:
Apply the row operation $R_{i} {k:signedcoef}R_1 \to R_{i}$ to

$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & {r2} & {r3} & {r4} \\ {a1} & {t2} & {t3} & {t4} \\ {b1} & {s2} & {s3} & {s4} \end{array}\right]$$

and enter the four entries of the new row {i}.
drills.solution:
Add ${k}$ times row 1 to row {i}, entry by entry, including the constant after the bar. Row {i} is $[\,{f} \;\; {w2} \;\; {w3} \mid {w4}\,]$ and ${k}$ times row 1 is $[\,{k} \;\; {k2} \;\; {k3} \mid {k4}\,]$.
Sum: **$[\,0 \;\; {n2} \;\; {n3} \mid {n4}\,]$**. The first entry becomes 0, which is the point of the operation: it clears column 1 below the leading 1.

drills.title: Solve a 2×2 system with an inverse matrix
drills.prompt: Write the system ${a:coef}x {b:signedcoef}y = {e1}$, ${c:coef}x {d:signedcoef}y = {e2}$ as $AX = B$ and solve it with $X = A^{-1}B$. Enter $\det A$, then $x$ and $y$.
drills.solution:
$A = \begin{bmatrix} {a} & {b} \\ {c} & {d} \end{bmatrix}$, so $\det A = ({a})({d}) - ({b})({c}) =$ **{det}**.
Swap the diagonal, negate the other two entries, and divide by the determinant: $A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{{det}}\begin{bmatrix} {d} & {nb} \\ {nc} & {a} \end{bmatrix}$.
Then $X = A^{-1}B = \dfrac{1}{{det}}\begin{bmatrix} ({d})({e1}) + ({nb})({e2}) \\ ({nc})({e1}) + ({a})({e2}) \end{bmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{{det}}\begin{bmatrix} {u} \\ {v} \end{bmatrix}$, so **$x = {xs}$** and **$y = {ys}$**.

drills.title: Zeros and multiplicity from a factored polynomial
drills.prompt: The graph shows $f(x) = {a:coef}(x {nr:signed})(x {ns:signed})^{{m}}(x {nt:signed})$. What is the degree of $f$, and what is the multiplicity of the zero at $x = {s}$?
drills.solution:
The degree is the sum of the multiplicities: $1 + {m} + 1 =$ **{deg}**.
The factor $(x {ns:signed})$ has exponent {m}, so $x = {s}$ has multiplicity **{m}**. (An even multiplicity touches the axis and turns back; an odd one crosses it, flattening out when it's 3 or more, as the graph shows.)

drills.title: Polynomial from zeros and a point
drills.prompt: Write the cubic polynomial with zeros ${r}$, ${s}$ and ${t}$ whose graph passes through $(0, {y0})$. (Factored form is fine.)
drills.solution:
$f(x) = a(x {nr:signed})(x {ns:signed})(x {nt:signed})$. At $x = 0$: $f(0) = a \cdot ({p0}) = {y0}$, so $a = {a}$.
**$f(x) = {a:coef}(x {nr:signed})(x {ns:signed})(x {nt:signed})$**.

drills.title: Synthetic division
drills.prompt: Divide $\;{a:coef}x^3 {b:signedcoef}x^2 {d:signedcoef}x {e:signed}$ by $x {nc:signed}$. Give the quotient and the remainder.
drills.solution:
Use $c = {c}$ with coefficients ${a}, {b}, {d}, {e}$. Bring down {a}; then ${t1}$ added to ${b}$ gives ${q1}$; ${t2}$ added to ${d}$ gives ${q0}$; ${t3}$ added to ${e}$ gives ${rem}$.
Quotient **${q2:coef}x^2 {q1:signedcoef}x {q0:signed}$**, remainder **{rem}**.

drills.title: Remainder theorem
drills.prompt: Find the remainder when $f(x) = {a:coef}x^4 {b:signedcoef}x^2 {d:signedcoef}x {e:signed}$ is divided by $x {nc:signed}$.
drills.solution: By the Remainder Theorem, the remainder is $f({c}) = {a}({c})^4 + ({b})({c})^2 + ({d})({c}) + ({e}) =$ **{rem}**.

drills.title: Find all zeros of a cubic
drills.prompt: Find all zeros of $\;x^3 {B:signedcoef}x^2 {C:signedcoef}x {D:signed}$, in increasing order. (All are integers.)
drills.solution:
Possible rational zeros are the divisors of {D}. Testing finds $f({r}) = 0$. Dividing by $x {nr:signed}$ leaves $x^2 {sb:signedcoef}x {sc:signed}$, which factors as $(x {ns:signed})(x {nt:signed})$.
Zeros: **{r}, {s}, {t}**.

drills.title: Cubic with a fractional zero

calc.mid: z + r + s - min(z, r, s) - max(z, r, s)

drills.prompt: Find all zeros of $\;{A}x^3 {B:signedcoef}x^2 {C:signedcoef}x {D:signed}$, in increasing order, as exact fractions.
drills.solution:
Candidates are $\pm$(factors of {D}) over (factors of {A}). The integer zeros {r} and {s} check out; dividing them out leaves the linear factor ${A}x - ({q})$, giving $x = {z:texfrac}$.
In increasing order: **${lo:texfrac}$, ${mid:texfrac}$, ${hi:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Simplify a square root
drills.prompt: Write $\sqrt{{n}}$ in simplest radical form $a\sqrt{\,b}$.
drills.solution: The largest perfect-square factor of {n} is {a2}: $\sqrt{{n}} = \sqrt{{a2} \cdot {b}} = \sqrt{{a2}}\sqrt{{b}} =$ **${a}\sqrt{{b}}$**.

drills.title: Evaluate a rational exponent
drills.prompt: Evaluate $\;{base}^{{p}/{q}}$. Give an exact answer (a fraction if needed).
drills.solution: The denominator {q} is the root: $\sqrt[{q}]{{base}} = {r}$. Then raise to the power {p}: ${r}^{{p}} =$ **${val:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Rationalize with a conjugate
drills.prompt: Rationalize the denominator and write $\dfrac{{c}}{{a} + \sqrt{{b}}}$ in the form $p + q\sqrt{{b}}$.
drills.solution:
Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate ${a} - \sqrt{{b}}$. The denominator becomes ${a}^2 - {b} = {den}$.
So the expression is $\dfrac{{c}({a} - \sqrt{{b}})}{{den}} = {m}({a} - \sqrt{{b}})$, giving $p =$ **{p}** and $q =$ **{q}**.

drills.title: Solve a radical equation
drills.prompt: Solve $\;\sqrt{{a:coef}x {b:signed}} {k:signed} = {rhs}$. Give an exact answer.
drills.solution:
Isolate the radical: $\sqrt{{a:coef}x {b:signed}} = {c}$. Square both sides: ${a:coef}x {b:signed} = {c2}$.
So ${a:coef}x = {cb}$ and $x =$ **${xs:texfrac}$**. Check: the radicand is ${c2}$ and its root is ${c}$, as required.

drills.title: Radical equation with an extraneous root
drills.prompt: Solve $\;\sqrt{x {p:signed}} = x {q:signed}$. Enter the valid solution and the extraneous value that squaring produces.
drills.solution:
Square both sides: $x {p:signed} = (x {q:signed})^2$, which rearranges to $x^2 {B:signedcoef}x {C:signed} = 0$, with roots ${s}$ and ${e}$.
Check: at $x = {s}$ the right side is ${sq} \ge 0$ and matches the root, so **{s}** is valid. At $x = {e}$ the right side is ${eq} < 0$, but a square root can't be negative, so **{e}** is extraneous.

drills.title: Rational exponent with an even numerator
drills.prompt: Solve $(x {h:signed})^{{m}/3} = {c}$. Enter both solutions, smaller first.
drills.solution:
Write the power with a cube root: $\left(\sqrt[3]{x {h:signed}}\right)^{{m}} = {c}$. The numerator {m} of the exponent is even, so undoing it gives both signs: $\sqrt[3]{x {h:signed}} = \pm {r}$.
Cube: $x {h:signed} = \pm {r3}$. So $x = {nh} - {r3} =$ **{s1}** or $x = {nh} + {r3} =$ **{s2}**.
Both check, since $({nr3})^{{m}/3} = ({nr})^{{m}} = {c}$ and $({r3})^{{m}/3} = {r}^{{m}} = {c}$. Raising both sides to the power $\tfrac{3}{{m}}$ alone would find only {s2}.

drills.title: Simplify a rational expression
drills.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{x^2 {nb:signedcoef}x {nc:signed}}{x^2 {db:signedcoef}x {dc:signed}}$.
drills.solution:
Factor both: $\dfrac{(x {p:signed})(x {q:signed})}{(x {p:signed})(x {r:signed})}$.
Cancel the common factor $(x {p:signed})$: **$\dfrac{x {q:signed}}{x {r:signed}}$** (with the original excluded values still excluded).

drills.title: Multiply rational expressions
drills.prompt: Multiply and simplify: $\dfrac{x^2 {s1:signedcoef}x {p1:signed}}{x^2 {s2:signedcoef}x {p2:signed}} \cdot \dfrac{x {c:signed}}{x {a:signed}}$
drills.solution:
Factor: $\dfrac{(x {a:signed})(x {b:signed})}{(x {c:signed})(x {d:signed})} \cdot \dfrac{x {c:signed}}{x {a:signed}}$.
Cancel $(x {a:signed})$ and $(x {c:signed})$: **$\dfrac{x {b:signed}}{x {d:signed}}$**.

drills.title: Add rational expressions
drills.prompt: Add and write as a single fraction: $\dfrac{{a}}{x {p:signed}} + \dfrac{{b}}{x {q:signed}}$
drills.solution:
The LCD is $(x {p:signed})(x {q:signed})$. Rewrite: $\dfrac{{a}(x {q:signed}) {b:signed}(x {p:signed})}{(x {p:signed})(x {q:signed})}$.
The numerator is ${a:coef}x {aq:signed} {b:signedcoef}x {bp:signed} = {A:coef}x {B:signed}$, so the sum is **$\dfrac{{A:coef}x {B:signed}}{(x {p:signed})(x {q:signed})}$**.

drills.title: Simplify a numeric complex fraction
drills.prompt: Simplify $\dfrac{\dfrac{{a}}{{b}} + \dfrac{{c}}{{d}}}{\dfrac{1}{{f}}}$ to an exact fraction.
drills.solution: The numerator is $\dfrac{{a}}{{b}} + \dfrac{{c}}{{d}} = {top:texfrac}$. Dividing by $\dfrac{1}{{f}}$ means multiplying by {f}: ${top:texfrac} \cdot {f} =$ **${val:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Solve a rational equation
drills.prompt: Solve $\;\dfrac{{a}}{x {p:signed}} = \dfrac{{b}}{x {q:signed}}$. Give an exact answer.
drills.solution:
Excluded values: $x \ne {np}$ and $x \ne {nq}$. Cross-multiply: ${a}(x {q:signed}) = {b}(x {p:signed})$.
So ${a:coef}x {aq:signed} = {b:coef}x {bp:signed}$, giving ${amb:coef}x = {rhs}$ and $x =$ **${xs:texfrac}$**, which isn't excluded.

drills.title: Working together
drills.prompt: One machine finishes a job in {t1} hours and another in {t2} hours. Working together, how many hours do they take? (Exact fraction.)
drills.solution:
Rates add: $\dfrac{1}{{t1}} + \dfrac{1}{{t2}} = \dfrac{1}{T}$. Multiply by ${t1} \cdot {t2} \cdot T$: ${t2}T + {t1}T = {pr}$.
So $T = \dfrac{{pr}}{{sm}} =$ **${tot:texfrac}$** hours.

drills.title: Boat speed against a current
drills.prompt: A boat travels {D1} km downstream in the same time it travels {D2} km upstream. The current flows at {c} km/h. What is the boat's speed in still water (km/h)?
drills.solution:
Equal times: $\dfrac{{D1}}{b + {c}} = \dfrac{{D2}}{b - {c}}$. Cross-multiply and solve: **{bs}** km/h.
Check: each trip takes {t} h.

drills.title: Asymptotes and intercepts of a rational function
drills.prompt: For $f(x) = \dfrac{{a:coef}x {b:signed}}{x {e:signed}}$, find the vertical asymptote, the horizontal asymptote, the $x$-intercept and the $y$-intercept. Give exact values.
drills.solution:
The denominator is zero at $x = {va}$, and the numerator there is not zero, so nothing cancels: vertical asymptote **$x = {va}$**.
Both degrees are 1, so the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of leading coefficients: **$y = {a}$**.
$x$-intercept: ${a:coef}x {b:signed} = 0$ gives **$x = {xi:texfrac}$**. $y$-intercept: $f(0) = \dfrac{{b}}{{e}} =$ **${yi:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Hole and vertical asymptote
drills.prompt: The graph of $g(x) = \dfrac{x^2 {n1:signedcoef}x {n0:signed}}{x^2 {d1:signedcoef}x {d0:signed}}$ has one hole and one vertical asymptote. Find the hole $(x, y)$ (exact) and the vertical asymptote.
drills.solution:
Factor: $g(x) = \dfrac{(x {nr:signed})(x {ns:signed})}{(x {nr:signed})(x {nt:signed})}$.
The common factor $(x {nr:signed})$ cancels, so there's a hole at $x = {r}$. Its height comes from the simplified form $\dfrac{x {ns:signed}}{x {nt:signed}}$: $\dfrac{{r} {ns:signed}}{{r} {nt:signed}} = {hy:texfrac}$. Hole: **$\left({r}, {hy:texfrac}\right)$**.
The factor $(x {nt:signed})$ remains in the denominator: vertical asymptote **$x = {t}$**.

drills.title: Inverse variation

choices.label: The time to finish a job varies inversely with the number of workers
The time to drive a fixed route varies inversely with the average speed
A quantity $y$ varies inversely with $x$

drills.prompt: {ctx}. When the input is {x1}, the output is {y1}. Find the output when the input is {x2}.
drills.solution:
Inverse variation means $y = \dfrac{k}{x}$, so the product is constant: $k = {x1} \cdot {y1} = {kc}$.
Then $y = \dfrac{{kc}}{{x2}} =$ **{y2}**.

drills.title: Sign chart for a cubic inequality

choices.label: \le
\ge

drills.prompt: Solve $(x {np:signed})(x {nq:signed})(x {nr:signed}) {rel} 0$ with a sign chart. Enter the three critical values from smallest to largest, then the number of integers from the smallest to the largest critical value (inclusive) that satisfy the inequality.
drills.solution:
Call the product $f(x)$. Its critical values are the zeros of the factors: **{lo}**, **{mid}** and **{hi}**.
Test one value in each interval: $f({t1}) = {v1}$, $f({t2}) = {v2}$, $f({t3}) = {v3}$, $f({t4}) = {v4}$. The signs alternate because each zero has multiplicity 1.
Keep the intervals whose sign makes $f(x) {rel} 0$ true, and include the critical values themselves only for $\le$ or $\ge$. Counting the integers from {lo} to {hi} in that solution gives **{cnt}**.

drills.title: Rational inequality with a constant

choices.label: \ge

calc.sm: if(m < n, if(rel == 1, m, m + 1), n + 1)
calc.lg: if(m < n, n - 1, if(rel == 1, m, m - 1))

drills.prompt: Solve $\dfrac{x {u:signed}}{x {nn:signed}} {rel} {k}$. Enter the smallest and the largest integer that satisfy the inequality.
drills.solution:
Don't multiply by $x {nn:signed}$ (its sign is unknown). Subtract {k} and use the common denominator:
$$\frac{x {u:signed} - {k}(x {nn:signed})}{x {nn:signed}} = \frac{{a1:coef}x {b1:signed}}{x {nn:signed}} {rel} 0.$$
Critical values: {m} (the numerator is 0) and {n} (the denominator is 0). A test value between them, $x = {tm}$, gives the original fraction $\approx {vt:num2}$, which is more than {k}; far to either side the left side of the last inequality is negative. So the solution is the interval between {n} and {m}: {n} is never included (the fraction has no value there), and {m} is included only for $\ge$.
Smallest integer solution **{sm}**, largest **{lg}**.

drills.title: When is the ball high enough?
drills.prompt: A ball's height after $t$ seconds is $h = -5t^2 + {v}t + {h0}$ meters. When does it first reach a height of {H} m, and for how many seconds is it at least {H} m high?
drills.solution:
Solve $-5t^2 + {v}t + {h0} \ge {H}$. Subtract {H}: $-5t^2 + {v}t {c0:signed} \ge 0$.
Divide by $-5$ and flip the symbol: $t^2 {bb:signedcoef}t {cc:signed} \le 0$, which factors as $(t - {t1})(t - {t2}) \le 0$.
The product is negative between its zeros and 0 at them, so ${t1} \le t \le {t2}$. The ball first reaches {H} m at **{t1} s** and stays at least that high for ${t2} - {t1} =$ **{gap} s**.

drills.title: Compound interest

choices.label: annually
quarterly
monthly

drills.prompt: You deposit {P:money0} at {rp}% annual interest, compounded {n}. What is the balance after {t} years (to the nearest cent)?
drills.solution:
Use $A = P\left(1 + \tfrac{\,r}{\,n}\right)^{n t}$ with $r = {r}$, {nn} compounding periods per year, and {nt} periods in all.
$A = {P:dp0}\left(1 + \dfrac{{r}}{{nn}}\right)^{{nt}} \approx$ **{A:money}**.

drills.title: Continuous compounding
drills.prompt: An account pays {rp}% interest compounded continuously. If you deposit {P:money0}, what is the balance after {t} years (to the nearest cent)?
drills.solution: $A = Pe^{r t} = {P:dp0}\,e^{{r} \cdot {t}} = {P:dp0}\,e^{{rtv:num4}} \approx$ **{A:money}**.

drills.title: Half-life
drills.prompt: A substance has a half-life of {h} days. Starting with {A0} g, how much remains after {t} days? (2 decimal places.)
drills.solution:
The number of half-lives is $\dfrac{{t}}{{h}} \approx {k:num4}$.
$A = {A0}\left(\tfrac12\right)^{{t}/{h}} \approx$ **{A:num2}** g.

drills.title: Evaluate a logarithm exactly
drills.prompt: Evaluate $\log_{{B}} {X:texfrac}$ exactly.
drills.solution: Write both as powers of {c}: ${B} = {c}^{{m}}$ and ${X:texfrac} = {c}^{{n}}$. We need $({c}^{{m}})^y = {c}^{{n}}$, so ${m}y = {n}$ and $y =$ **${val:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Combine logarithms
drills.prompt: Simplify $\log_{{b}} {M} + \log_{{b}} {N} - \log_{{b}} {P}$ to a single number.
drills.solution: Product and quotient rules: $\log_{{b}} \dfrac{{M} \cdot {N}}{{P}}$. The argument is $\dfrac{{M} \cdot {N}}{{P}} = {b}^{{k}}$, so the value is **{k}**.

drills.title: Change of base
drills.prompt: Evaluate $\log_{{b}} {x}$ to three decimal places.
drills.solution: Change of base: $\log_{{b}} {x} = \dfrac{\ln {x}}{\ln {b}} \approx \dfrac{{lx:num4}}{{lb:num4}} \approx$ **{val:dp3}**.

drills.title: Exponential equation with a common base
drills.prompt: Solve $\;{B1}^{x {p:signed}} = {B2}^{x}$. Give an exact answer.
drills.solution:
Write both sides as powers of {c}: ${c}^{{m:coef}(x {p:signed})} = {c}^{{n:coef}x}$.
Equate exponents: ${m:coef}x {mp:signed} = {n:coef}x$, so ${nm:coef}x = {mp}$ and $x =$ **${xs:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Solve an exponential equation with logarithms
drills.prompt: Solve $\;{a} \cdot {b}^{x} {c:signed} = {d}$. Give $x$ to three decimal places.
drills.solution:
Isolate the power: ${a} \cdot {b}^x = {dc}$, so ${b}^x = {q:num4}$.
Take $\ln$ of both sides: $x = \dfrac{\ln {q:num4}}{\ln {b}} \approx$ **{xs:dp3}**.

drills.title: Solve a logarithmic equation
drills.prompt: Solve $\;\log_{{b}}({a:coef}x {c:signed}) = {k}$. Give an exact answer.
drills.solution:
Exponential form: ${a:coef}x {c:signed} = {b}^{{k}} = {bk}$.
So ${a:coef}x = {rhs}$ and $x =$ **${xs:texfrac}$**. The argument equals {bk}, which is positive, so the solution checks.

drills.title: nth term of an arithmetic sequence
drills.prompt: For the arithmetic sequence ${a1}, {a2}, {a3}, \ldots$, find the term $a_{{n}}$.

drills.title: Sum of an arithmetic series
drills.prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{{n}} ({c:coef}k {k0:signed})$.
drills.solution:
The terms form an arithmetic sequence from $a_1 = {first}$ to $a_{{n}} = {last}$, with {n} terms.
$S = \dfrac{n(a_1 + a_n)}{2} = \dfrac{{n}({first} + ({last}))}{2} =$ **{S}**.

drills.title: Arithmetic sequence from two terms
drills.prompt: An arithmetic sequence has $a_{{p}} = {ap}$ and $a_{{q}} = {aq}$. Find the common difference and the first term.
drills.solution:
From term {p} to term {q} is {steps} steps: ${steps}d = {aq} - ({ap}) = {diff}$, so $d =$ **{d}**.
Then $a_1 = a_{{p}} - ({p} - 1)d$, which gives $a_1 =$ **{a1}**.

drills.title: nth term of a geometric sequence
drills.prompt: For the geometric sequence ${a1}, {a2}, {a3}, \ldots$, find the term $a_{{n}}$ (exact fraction if needed).

drills.title: Sum of a geometric series
drills.prompt: Find the sum of the first {n} terms of the geometric sequence with $a_1 = {a1}$ and $r = {r}$.

drills.title: Infinite geometric series
drills.prompt: Find the sum of the infinite geometric series ${a1} + \left({a2:texfrac}\right) + \cdots$ with ratio $r = {r:texfrac}$. (Exact fraction.)
drills.solution: $|r| < 1$, so the series converges: $S = \dfrac{a_1}{1 - r} = \dfrac{{a1}}{{omr:texfrac}} =$ **${S:texfrac}$**.

drills.title: Permutations (order matters)
drills.prompt: {n} runners finish a race with no ties. In how many different ways can the first {r} places be filled?
drills.solution:
First, second, third… are different places, so order matters: use a permutation.
$_{{n}}P_{{r}} = \dfrac{{n}!}{({n} - {r})!} = \dfrac{{n}!}{{nr}!}$, which is the product of the {r} numbers counting down from {n}: **{ans:int}**.
(Ignoring order would give only {c:int} groups of finishers.)

drills.title: Combinations (order doesn't matter)
drills.prompt: A teacher picks a group of {r} students from a class of {n} to work together on a project. How many different groups are possible?
drills.solution:
A group has no first or second member, so order doesn't matter: use a combination.
$_{{n}}C_{{r}} = \dfrac{{n}!}{{r}!\,{nr}!} =$ **{ans:int}**.
Counting ordered selections would give {p:int}, which lists each group {r}! = {rf} times; {p:int} ÷ {rf} = {ans:int}.

drills.title: Committees from two groups
drills.prompt: A committee is made up of {a} of the {J} juniors and {b} of the {S} seniors in a club. How many different committees are possible?
drills.solution:
Choose the juniors: $_{{J}}C_{{a}} = {cj}$ ways. Choose the seniors: $_{{S}}C_{{b}} = {cs}$ ways.
Every choice of juniors goes with every choice of seniors, so multiply (counting principle): ${cj} \times {cs} =$ **{ans:int}**.

drills.title: Addition rule and complement
drills.prompt: For a randomly chosen student, the probability of taking art is $P(A) = {PA}$, of taking band is $P(B) = {PB}$, and of taking both is $P(A \text{ and } B) = {PAB}$. Find the probability the student takes art or band, and the probability the student takes neither.
drills.solution:
Adding ${PA} + {PB} = {sumab}$ counts the students in both twice, so subtract the overlap once:
$P(A \text{ or } B) = {PA} + {PB} - {PAB} =$ **{ans}**.
"Neither" is the complement of "art or band": $1 - {ans} =$ **{none}**.

drills.title: Conditional probability from a two-way table
drills.prompt:
Students took the same course online or in person:

| | Passed | Did not pass | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Online | {a} | {b} | {r1} |
| In person | {c} | {d} | {r2} |
| Total | {c1} | {c2} | {tot} |

For a randomly chosen student, find $P(\text{passed} \mid \text{online})$ and $P(\text{online} \mid \text{passed})$ as fractions in lowest terms.
drills.solution:
Given "online", use only the Online row ({r1} students), of whom {a} passed: $\dfrac{{a}}{{r1}} =$ **${p1:texfrac}$**.
Given "passed", use only the Passed column ({c1} students), of whom {a} were online: $\dfrac{{a}}{{c1}} =$ **${p2:texfrac}$**.
Same numerator, different denominators: the condition decides which total you divide by.

drills.title: Probability by counting (draws without replacement)
drills.prompt: A bag holds {r} red and {bl} blue marbles. You draw {k} marbles at random without replacement. What is the probability that all {k} are red? Give an exact fraction in lowest terms.
drills.solution:
Every set of {k} marbles is equally likely. There are $_{{n}}C_{{k}} = {bot}$ ways to choose {k} of the {n} marbles, and $_{{r}}C_{{k}} = {top}$ ways to choose {k} of the {r} red ones.
$P(\text{all red}) = \dfrac{{top}}{{bot}} =$ **${ans:texfrac}$**.
(Multiplying along a tree gives the same answer: the first draw is red with probability $\tfrac{{r}}{{n}}$, and each later draw has one fewer red and one fewer marble.)

drills.title: The 68–95–99.7 rule
drills.prompt: A measurement is approximately normal with mean {mu} and standard deviation {sd}. Use the 68–95–99.7 rule to estimate the percent of values between {lo} and {hi}.
drills.solution:
{lo} is at $z = {k1}$ and {hi} is at $z = {k2}$: that many standard deviations from the mean.
From the rule, the percent of values below each mark is: $\mu - 3\sigma$: 0.15%, $\mu - 2\sigma$: 2.5%, $\mu - \sigma$: 16%, $\mu$: 50%, $\mu + \sigma$: 84%, $\mu + 2\sigma$: 97.5%, $\mu + 3\sigma$: 99.85%.
So the percent between {lo} and {hi} is {F2}% − {F1}% = **{ans}%**.

drills.title: z-scores and normal probabilities
drills.prompt: A measurement is normally distributed with mean {mu} and standard deviation {sd}. Find the z-scores of {lo} and {hi}, then the probability that a value is between {lo} and {hi} (4 decimal places).
drills.solution:
$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$: for {lo}, $z = \dfrac{{lo} - {mu}}{{sd}} =$ **{z1}**; for {hi}, $z = \dfrac{{hi} - {mu}}{{sd}} =$ **{z2}**.
The area to the left of $z = {z2}$ is {A2:dp4} and to the left of $z = {z1}$ is {A1:dp4}, so the area between is {A2:dp4} − {A1:dp4} ≈ **{P:dp4}**.
On a calculator: normalcdf({lo}, {hi}, {mu}, {sd}).

drills.title: Margin of error of a poll
drills.prompt: In a random sample of {n:int} voters, {ph}% support a ballot measure. Estimate the margin of error using $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt n}$, as a percent to 1 decimal place, and give the likely range of support among all voters.
drills.solution:
$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{{n:dp0}}} \approx {fr:dp4}$, which is {moe:num2}%. So the margin of error is about **{moe:num1}%**.
The likely range for all voters is {ph}% ± {moe:num1}%: from **{lo:num1}%** to **{hi:num1}%**.

drills.title: Expand a binomial to the 4th power
drills.prompt: Expand $({a:coef}x {b:signed})^4$. Enter the coefficients of $x^4$, $x^3$, $x^2$ and $x$, and the constant term.
drills.solution:
Row 4 of Pascal's triangle is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1. The first term is ${a:coef}x$ and the second is ${b}$; keep each in parentheses so its coefficient and sign are raised to the power:
$$({a:coef}x)^4 + 4({a:coef}x)^3({b}) + 6({a:coef}x)^2({b})^2 + 4({a:coef}x)({b})^3 + ({b})^4$$
$$= {c4:coef}x^4 {c3:signedcoef}x^3 {c2:signedcoef}x^2 {c1:signedcoef}x {c0:signed}.$$
The coefficients are **{c4}**, **{c3}**, **{c2}**, **{c1}** and **{c0}**.

drills.title: One coefficient of a binomial expansion
drills.prompt: Find the coefficient of $x^{{j}}$ in the expansion of $({a:coef}x {b:signed})^{{n}}$.
drills.solution:
Each term is $_{{n}}C_k\,({a:coef}x)^{{n} - k}\,({b})^k$, and the power of $x$ is ${n} - k$. For $x^{{j}}$ you need $k = {k}$.
The term is $_{{n}}C_{{k}}\,({a:coef}x)^{{j}}\,({b})^{{k}} = {C} \cdot ({pa}) \cdot ({pb})\,x^{{j}}$, so the coefficient is **{ans}**.

drills.title: A given term of a binomial expansion
drills.prompt: Find term number {r} (counting the first term as term 1) in the expansion of $(x {c:signedcoef}y)^{{n}}$. Type it using $x$ and $y$, for example 60x^3y^2.
drills.solution:
The terms are numbered from $k = 0$, so term {r} has $k = {k}$:
$$_{{n}}C_{{k}}\,x^{{nk}}\,({c:coef}y)^{{k}} = {C} \cdot x^{{nk}} \cdot ({ck})\,y^{{k}}.$$
The term is **${T:dp0}x^{{nk}}y^{{k}}$**.

drills.title: Converting degrees and radians
drills.prompt: Convert ${deg}^\circ$ to radians (exact: type pi for $\pi$), and convert $\dfrac{{rnum:coef}\pi}{{rden}}$ radians to degrees.
drills.solution:
Degrees to radians: multiply by $\dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ}$. ${deg}^\circ \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{180^\circ} = {k:texfrac}\pi$, so the answer is **${k:texfrac}\pi$** (about {rad:num2}).
Radians to degrees: multiply by $\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}$. The $\pi$'s cancel: $\dfrac{{rnum:coef}\pi}{{rden}} \cdot \dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \dfrac{{rnum} \cdot 180^\circ}{{rden}} =$ **{dd}°**.

drills.title: Coterminal and reference angles
drills.prompt: Find the angle between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$ that is coterminal with ${th}^\circ$, and give its reference angle in degrees.
drills.solution:
Add or subtract full turns of $360^\circ$ until the angle lands in $[0^\circ, 360^\circ)$: ${th}^\circ {adj:signed}^\circ =$ **{co}°**.
{co}° is in quadrant {quad}. The reference angle is the acute angle between the terminal side and the $x$-axis
(quadrant 1: $\theta$; 2: $180^\circ - \theta$; 3: $\theta - 180^\circ$; 4: $360^\circ - \theta$), which here is **{ref}°**.

drills.title: Sine and cosine of special angles

choices.label: $30^\circ$ is in quadrant I with reference angle $30^\circ$, where $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac12$ and $\cos 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. In quadrant I both are positive, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac12$ and $\cos\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$45^\circ$ is in quadrant I with reference angle $45^\circ$, where $\sin 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. In quadrant I both are positive, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

$60^\circ$ is in quadrant I with reference angle $60^\circ$, where $\sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$. In quadrant I both are positive, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = \tfrac12$.
$90^\circ$ is a quadrantal angle; its terminal side meets the unit circle at $(0, 1)$, so $\sin\theta = 1$ and $\cos\theta = 0$.

$120^\circ$ is in quadrant II with reference angle $60^\circ$, where $\sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$. In quadrant II sine is positive and cosine is negative, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = -\tfrac12$.

$135^\circ$ is in quadrant II with reference angle $45^\circ$, where $\sin 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. In quadrant II sine is positive and cosine is negative, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

$150^\circ$ is in quadrant II with reference angle $30^\circ$, where $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac12$ and $\cos 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. In quadrant II sine is positive and cosine is negative, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac12$ and $\cos\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$210^\circ$ is in quadrant III with reference angle $30^\circ$, where $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac12$ and $\cos 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. In quadrant III both are negative, so $\sin\theta = -\tfrac12$ and $\cos\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$225^\circ$ is in quadrant III with reference angle $45^\circ$, where $\sin 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. In quadrant III both are negative, so $\sin\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

$240^\circ$ is in quadrant III with reference angle $60^\circ$, where $\sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$. In quadrant III both are negative, so $\sin\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = -\tfrac12$.
$270^\circ$ is a quadrantal angle; its terminal side meets the unit circle at $(0, -1)$, so $\sin\theta = -1$ and $\cos\theta = 0$.

$300^\circ$ is in quadrant IV with reference angle $60^\circ$, where $\sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$. In quadrant IV sine is negative and cosine is positive, so $\sin\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = \tfrac12$.

$315^\circ$ is in quadrant IV with reference angle $45^\circ$, where $\sin 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. In quadrant IV sine is negative and cosine is positive, so $\sin\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

$330^\circ$ is in quadrant IV with reference angle $30^\circ$, where $\sin 30^\circ = \tfrac12$ and $\cos 30^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$. In quadrant IV sine is negative and cosine is positive, so $\sin\theta = -\tfrac12$ and $\cos\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

$-60^\circ$ is coterminal with $300^\circ$. $300^\circ$ is in quadrant IV with reference angle $60^\circ$, where $\sin 60^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos 60^\circ = \tfrac12$. In quadrant IV sine is negative and cosine is positive, so $\sin\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = \tfrac12$.

$-135^\circ$ is coterminal with $225^\circ$. $225^\circ$ is in quadrant III with reference angle $45^\circ$, where $\sin 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. In quadrant III both are negative, so $\sin\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = -\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

$405^\circ$ is coterminal with $45^\circ$. $45^\circ$ is in quadrant I with reference angle $45^\circ$, where $\sin 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos 45^\circ = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$. In quadrant I both are positive, so $\sin\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$ and $\cos\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

drills.prompt: Find the exact values of $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ for $\theta = {ang:int}^\circ = {k:texfrac}\pi$. Type roots like sqrt(3)/2.
drills.solution:
{ang}
The point on the unit circle is $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta) \approx ({c:dp3}, {s:dp3})$.

drills.title: Amplitude, period and midline from an equation

choices.label: 2\pi
\pi
\tfrac{2\pi}{3}
\tfrac{\pi}{2}
4\pi
\sin
\cos

drills.prompt: For $y = {a:coef}{fn}({bb:coef}x) {kk:signed}$, find the amplitude, the period (type pi for $\pi$), the midline $y = k$, and the maximum and minimum values.
drills.solution:
Compare with $y = a{fn}(bx) + k$: $a = {a}$, $b = {bb:num4}$, $k = {kk}$.
Amplitude $|a| =$ **{amp}**. Period $\dfrac{2\pi}{b} = \dfrac{2\pi}{{bb:num4}} =$ **${bb}$** (about {per:num2}). Midline $y =$ **{kk}**.
Maximum $= k + |a| = {kk} + {amp} =$ **{mx}**; minimum $= k - |a| = {kk} - {amp} =$ **{mn}**.

drills.title: Equation of a sinusoid from its graph

choices.label: maximum, which is how cosine starts, so the graph is not flipped:
minimum, so the cosine graph is flipped:

drills.prompt: The graph shows a sinusoid $y = a\cos(bx) + k$. Find $a$, $b$ (type pi for $\pi$) and $k$.
drills.solution:
The highest value is {mxv} and the lowest is {mnv}. Midline: $k = \dfrac{{mxv} + ({mnv})}{2} =$ **{kk}**. Amplitude: $\dfrac{{mxv} - ({mnv})}{2} = {A}$.
The graph returns to its starting value at $x = {P}$, so the period is {P} and $b = \dfrac{2\pi}{{P}} =$ **${bk:texfrac}\pi$**.
At $x = 0$ the graph is at a {sgn} $a =$ **{av}**.

drills.title: Ferris wheel model
drills.prompt: A Ferris wheel {D} m across has its center {c} m above the ground and turns once every {T} minutes. You board at the bottom at $t = 0$. Model your height as $h(t) = a\cos(bt) + k$: find $a$, $b$ (type pi for $\pi$), $k$, and your height after {t} minutes (to 0.1 m).
drills.solution:
The radius {R} m is the amplitude, and the center height {c} m is the midline, so $k =$ **{c}**.
You start at the lowest point, which is how $-\cos$ starts, so $a =$ **{am}**.
One turn takes {T} minutes, so $b = \dfrac{2\pi}{{T}} =$ **${bk:texfrac}\pi$**.
$h({t}) = {am}\cos\left({bk:texfrac}\pi \cdot {t}\right) + {c} \approx$ **{h:num1}** m (calculator in radian mode).
